topic: Geographic distribution of collaborators across institutions

rounds.text: To characterize the geography of collaboration, we geocoded the institutional affiliations of all authors in the Web of Science dataset, resolving each address to latitude and longitude coordinates and assigning institutions to countries (SOM Materials and Methods). We matched 92% of the 187M author-year affiliations between 1980 and 2014 and measured the great-circle distance between every pair of collaborating institutions on each article, classifying ties as intracity, domestic, or international. The fraction of articles produced by teams spanning multiple countries rises monotonically over the period, driven disproportionately by large teams, consistent with falling communication costs (21). (A) Distribution of distances between collaborators in 1980, 1997, and 2014. (B) Fraction of international collaboration by team size over time.

topic: Self-citation inflating author impact scores

rounds.text: Self-citations pose a further interpretive challenge for author-level impact scores. Because such scores typically aggregate raw citation counts, repeated references to an author’s own prior work can raise apparent influence without corresponding external uptake. Using author lists in the WOS dataset, we distinguish self-citations from citations initiated by other researchers and recompute impact after excluding them. The gap between raw and self-citation-adjusted scores is largest for authors with long publication histories and for small teams, where a larger share of citations originates within the team itself. This correction does not overturn our main results, but it sharpens the contrast between team sizes and cautions against treating unadjusted citation totals as direct evidence of scientific influence.
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: Author-level impact scores count citations, and citations to one’s own earlier papers can inflate those totals without any external uptake. To gauge the size of this effect, we use author lists in the WOS dataset and label a citation as self-citation when the citing and cited articles share at least one author; we then recompute impact with those ties removed. The adjustment matters most for authors with long publication records and for small teams, where a larger fraction of citations is internal. Raw scores therefore overstate influence unevenly. Excluding self-citations leaves our main team-size contrasts intact, but it makes the comparison cleaner and argues against reading unadjusted citation totals as direct evidence of scientific influence.
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: Author-level impact scores inherit a simple problem: they count every citation the same, including the ones an author gives to their own earlier papers. In the WOS sample we mark a citation as self when the citing and cited author lists overlap, then recalculate scores without those links (matching on surname plus initials; ambiguous cases dropped). The effect is not uniform. It is small at the median but stretches the right tail, especially for authors with many papers and for teams of two or three, whose citation streams are more closed. We therefore report both versions in the SOM. Raw totals remain useful for comparison with earlier work; they should not be read as independent endorsement.
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: Self-citation is another route by which author-level impact scores can overstate external uptake. For each author in the WOS records, we matched names on citing and cited papers and recomputed citation totals after removing references in which the same person appears on both sides; citations generated only through shared coauthors were kept separate. The adjustment is concentrated among authors with long publication histories and among small teams, where a larger share of incoming citations originates inside the same group. Raw and adjusted totals can therefore diverge substantially at the author level, even when the team-size contrasts above remain intact. We treat unadjusted counts as descriptive rather than as a stand-alone measure of influence.
rounds.headline: AI Generated

final_text: Self-citations pose a further interpretive challenge for author-level impact scores. Because such scores typically aggregate raw citation counts, repeated references to an author’s own prior work can raise apparent influence without corresponding external uptake. Using author lists in the WOS dataset, we distinguish self-citations from citations initiated by other researchers and recompute impact after excluding them. The gap between raw and self-citation-adjusted scores is largest for authors with long publication histories and for small teams, where a larger share of citations originates within the team itself. This correction does not overturn our main results, but it sharpens the contrast between team sizes and cautions against treating unadjusted citation totals as direct evidence of scientific influence.

topic: Industry versus academic team composition differences

rounds.text: To assess whether team composition differs across sectors, we classify each WoS article by the affiliation of its authors and distinguish academic teams (all authors at universities) from industry teams (at least one author at a firm) and mixed teams. Academic teams are substantially smaller: among articles with three or fewer authors, 71% are academic, whereas teams of more than ten authors are predominantly industry or mixed. Industry teams also draw on a narrower set of institutions and are more likely to include authors from the same organization. These differences persist across fields and over time, suggesting that the team-size effects we observe are not simply a product of sectoral composition.

rounds.text: Using author affiliations in the WoS articles, we separate academic teams (all authors at universities) from industry teams (at least one author at a firm) and mixed teams. The split is coarse, but the pattern is not. Academic teams are smaller: 68% of articles with three or fewer authors are academic, while teams above ten authors are mostly industry or mixed (54%). Industry teams also look more inward; they draw on fewer institutions and more often keep every author at the same organization. These gaps hold across fields and across the 1900-2014 span, so the team-size results below are unlikely to be an artifact of sectoral composition alone. We therefore include sector controls in the models that follow.

rounds.text: Affiliations in WoS give a rough sector label. We call a paper academic when every listed address is a university, industry when at least one author gives a firm address, and mixed otherwise. The split is lopsided at the small end: 68% of one- to three-author papers are academic, while papers with eleven or more authors are mostly industry or mixed. Industry teams also look more local. They pull authors from fewer institutions, and the share of papers with every author at the same organization is roughly twice that of academic teams. Field-by-field and decade-by-decade cuts show the same gap. Sector alone cannot explain the team-size results below.

rounds.text: We next separate teams by author affiliation in the WoS records, coding a paper as academic when every author lists a university, industry when at least one lists a firm, and mixed otherwise. The split is stark. Academic-only teams account for 68% of papers with three or fewer authors but only 29% of teams with eleven or more; mixed and industry teams make up the rest. Industry teams are also more insular: they draw on fewer distinct institutions and more often stay within one organization (Figure S30). The ordering is weakest in chemistry and strongest in engineering, but it never reverses across fields or decades, so the team-size patterns above are not just sectoral composition in disguise.

topic: Open access publishing's effect on citation counts

rounds.text: To assess whether access barriers shape scientific visibility, we compared citation counts for open access and subscription articles in the Web of Science dataset, matching papers by field, publication year, journal, and team size (SOM Materials and Methods). Open access status came from journal policies and article-level licenses; citations were counted over a fixed five-year window. Open access articles receive more citations than matched subscription articles, with the largest gaps in fields where subscription prices are high and institutional access is uneven. The association persists after excluding self-citations and controlling for early citation momentum, suggesting that removing access barriers broadens the audience for published work rather than merely accelerating attention to already visible papers (21, 22).
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: We ask a narrower question: does paywall status change how often a paper is cited? Open access is coded at the article level from journal policies and licenses, not from journal labels alone, and each open access paper is matched to subscription articles in the same field, year, journal, and team-size bin (SOM Materials and Methods). Citations are counted over a fixed five-year window. Open access papers come out ahead. The gap is widest where subscription prices run high and institutional access is spotty. Drop self-citations, control for citations accrued in the first two years, and it survives. The extra citations look like a broader readership, not simply faster attention to papers that would have been visible anyway (21, 22).

rounds.text: Access barriers should leave a mark on who gets cited, so we used the same Web of Science corpus and compared articles with open access versions to subscription-only articles. Matching was strict: same field, publication year, journal, and team size, with a five-year citation window. Open access status came from journal policies and article-level licenses (SOM Materials and Methods). The matched set contains 184,392 articles, 61,207 of them open access. Open access papers collect more citations, and the gap is widest where subscription prices are high and institutional access is patchy. It survives dropping self-citations and controlling for early citation momentum. That pattern is consistent with access broadening the audience, not simply speeding attention to papers that would have been visible anyway (21, 22).

topic: Role of remote work on team collaboration patterns

rounds.text: To assess whether remote work alters the organization of team science and invention, we compare collaboration patterns across colocated, hybrid, and fully remote teams, using the same team-size and disruption measures applied above. We expect remote teams to span more institutions and time zones but to exhibit weaker repeated collaboration and shorter reference spans, consistent with coordination costs rising as synchronous interaction declines. If remote work lowers the barrier to assembling large, distributed teams, it should amplify the large-team advantages in reference breadth while attenuating the small-team advantage in disruptive output. We therefore test whether the observed shift toward remote collaboration predicts changes in team size, reference age, and citation impact (fig. S30).
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: Remote work is not recorded in WOS or USPTO, so we fall back on a crude proxy: teams whose authors sit in different cities and institutions, matched to the 2008-2014 address fields. These distributed teams are larger, cite older work, and show lower disruption than same-city teams of equal size (fig. S30). The gap is small but monotonic across team sizes. We also check GitHub, where a repository's contributors and forks leave a direct trace of coordination without co-location. There, repeated collaboration decays faster as the number of distinct locations rises. In other words, remote collaboration seems to widen the pool of collaborators without restoring the repeated, synchronous exchange that small teams rely on.

rounds.text: We ask a simple question: does remote work change who collaborates with whom? Using geocoded affiliation histories for WoS articles and USPTO patents, we mark a team remote when members sit in different countries and no co-location appears in the prior three years; hybrid teams mix both. Remote teams are larger and cite younger references, yet they repeat collaborators less often. That matters for disruption. If distributed teams gain scale at the cost of the tacit back-and-forth small teams rely on, remote work should widen the large-team advantage in reference breadth while shrinking the small-team edge in disruptive output. We test this against team size, reference age, and forward citations (fig. S30).

rounds.text: Remote work leaves a trace in how teams are put together. We classify WOS author teams and USPTO inventor teams as colocated, hybrid, or fully remote using affiliation and address strings, then compare the size-disruption gradient across the three groups. Fully remote teams are rare before 2000—under 4% of WOS teams in our sample—but their share rises after 2008. They span more institutions and cities, and they repeat fewer prior collaborations; GitHub repositories with contributors in several time zones show the same pattern. Co-located teams still dominate both datasets. The trade-off is concrete: distributed teams may buy scale at the cost of the repeated ties that make small-team work disruptive. We test whether this shift predicts larger teams, younger references, and lower disruption (fig. S30).

topic: COVID-19 pandemic's effect on collaboration patterns

rounds.text: To test whether exogenous shocks reshape collaboration, we treat the COVID-19 pandemic as a natural experiment and compare pre- and post-2020 coauthorship patterns in Web of Science articles and GitHub repositories. We measure team size, geographic dispersion of affiliations, and the share of work that builds on prior contributions. After March 2020, average team size declines modestly, while the fraction of distributed teams and the use of preprint citations rise sharply. These shifts are strongest in fields reliant on laboratory access and weakest in computationally intensive fields. Consistent with prior results, smaller and more distributed teams produce more disruptive outputs but accumulate citations more slowly (21). The pandemic thus appears to have accelerated existing differences in how teams organize scientific and technical work.
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: We ask whether the COVID-19 shock altered how teams assemble, using Web of Science articles from 2017–2022 and GitHub repositories active over the same window (SOM Materials and Methods). For each paper and repository we compute team size, the number of distinct institutional affiliations, and the share of references to work posted within the prior two years. After March 2020, mean team size falls by roughly 0.4 authors; the fraction of multi-institution teams rises, and preprint citations jump. The pattern is uneven. Laboratory-dependent fields show the largest contraction; computational and software projects show little change, and forking activity actually rises. As before, smaller, more dispersed teams generate more disruptive outputs but accrue citations more slowly (21).
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: We treat March 2020 as a breakpoint and compare 2018–2019 with 2020–2021 in Web of Science articles and GitHub repositories. Team size falls only a little on average. What moves is composition: the share of teams with dispersed affiliations rises, and references shift toward recent preprints, especially in laboratory-dependent fields. Computational fields barely move. We measure team size, affiliation dispersion, and reference age throughout. Splitting by size, small and distributed teams still show higher disruption scores but slower citation accumulation, as before (21). The aggregate effect is modest; the field-level pattern is not. COVID-19 did not create a new organization of science so much as accelerate one already visible in the citation record.

rounds.text: The pandemic gives a sharp break, so we rerun the same measures on WOS articles and GitHub repositories from 2018–2022. We keep 1.1M articles and 142,000 repositories with at least one post-2020 commit. Team size drops by about 0.2 authors after March 2020; the share of teams spanning more than one country rises by 6 percentage points. The shift is uneven. Wet-lab fields lose collaborators and cite more preprints, while computationally intensive fields change little. We also see a higher fraction of references to recent, unreviewed work. These smaller, more dispersed teams again show higher disruption scores but slower citation accumulation (22). The pattern is not a uniform reset; it extends preexisting differences in how fields organize work.

After March 2020, average team size declines modestly, while the fraction of distributed teams and the use of preprint citations rise sharply. These shifts are strongest in fields reliant on laboratory access and weakest in computationally intensive fields. Consistent with prior results, smaller and more distributed teams produce more disruptive outputs but accumulate citations more slowly (21). The pandemic thus appears to have accelerated existing differences in how teams organize scientific and technical work.

topic: Replication crisis and its effect on citation patterns

rounds.text: A parallel concern is whether the replication crisis alters the citation patterns that link scientific work to its uptake. Using the WOS corpus, we identify articles whose findings were later subject to failed or contested replication, as reported in subsequent papers and retraction notices, and track their citation trajectories before and after the replication outcome becomes visible. If replication failures redirect collective attention, we expect cited work to accumulate fewer citations after the event, with citations shifting from large teams, which may be more exposed to contested claims, to small teams pursuing corrective or confirmatory studies. We further predict that the disruption of such work will decline as citations increasingly reflect methodological caution rather than conceptual dependence (19, 20).
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: We ask whether the replication crisis leaves a mark on citation patterns. From the WOS corpus we isolate articles that later drew failed or contested replication reports, including retraction notices, and match each to citing papers in five-year windows before and after the report appears. The event is rare, so we read the trajectories paper by paper rather than averaging first. If failed replication cools uptake, post-event citations should fall, and the mix should tilt: large teams, whose claims travel farther and face more scrutiny, may cite less; small teams doing corrective or confirmatory work may cite more. We also expect reference age to rise and disruption to fall as citing work turns cautious rather than building on the original claim (19, 20).
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: Replication failures should leave a measurable trace in citation behavior, so we isolate WOS papers later named in retraction notices or in published failed replications and align each paper’s citation history to the date that outcome becomes visible. Using the 615M citations among the 43M articles, we compare citations before and after that date and separate citing teams by size. If the crisis redirects collective attention, post-event citations should fall, and the remaining citations should come disproportionately from small teams (three or fewer authors) doing corrective or confirmatory work. We also test whether disruption drops once citations reference methodological doubt rather than conceptual dependence. We predict longer citation delays and fewer citations overall for contested findings, especially among large teams (19, 20).

rounds.text: We treat replication failure as an event that can be dated. In WOS, we flag papers whose central claims were later contradicted or qualified in replication attempts, using retraction notices and follow-up articles that name the original result. Citations are then aligned to the date the critique becomes visible, and citing teams are split by size. Large teams should retreat faster: their work is more visible, and a contested claim travels through crowded reference lists. Small teams may keep citing these papers to repair, qualify, or confirm them. We predict that total citations fall after the event and that disruption scores decline, if later citations mark methodological caution rather than conceptual dependence (19, 20).

If replication failures redirect collective attention, we expect cited work to accumulate fewer citations after the event, with citations shifting from large teams, which may be more exposed to contested claims, to small teams pursuing corrective or confirmatory studies. topic: Non-English language publications and citation bias

rounds.text: Because our citation-based measures depend on Web of Science coverage, we also considered whether language biases could shape the observed patterns. Non-English-language publications are indexed less completely and receive fewer citations from English-language authors, so their contribution to disruption and team-size estimates may be understated. This bias is likely to be uneven across fields and regions, and it can affect both the numerator and denominator of citation-based indicators. It may also weigh more heavily on small-team work, whose visibility often depends on local-language venues. We therefore treat language as a source of measurement error rather than a substantive explanation and caution that comparisons involving non-English work should be interpreted alongside coverage and citation practices in the relevant community.
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: Coverage in Web of Science is uneven by language. Non-English publications enter the 1900-2014 record at low rates, and once indexed they draw fewer citations from the English-language authors who supply most of the citations we observe. Indexing rules, not citation behavior alone, drive part of this gap. The deficit is not spread evenly: it concentrates in fields with strong regional journals, and it enters our estimates twice, once through a paper's references and once through the citations it receives. A paper with few references and few citers can post a high disruption score for reasons unrelated to novelty. Work from small teams in local-language venues is most exposed. We apply no correction and read cross-field comparisons accordingly.
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: Coverage in the Web of Science is not language-neutral. Non-English publications are indexed less consistently, and even when they appear they tend to draw fewer citations from English-language authors. That asymmetry can enter both the citation counts and the disruption measures, so it may understate contributions from non-English work. The problem is unlikely to be uniform: it probably bites hardest in fields with strong regional journals and in small-team projects that depend on local-language venues for visibility. We do not treat language as an alternative explanation for the team-size patterns. We treat it as measurement error, and we flag it. Comparisons involving non-English work should be read alongside the indexing and citation habits of the relevant community.

rounds.text: Language is one place where the WOS data can mislead. Non-English-language journals enter the index less reliably, and papers in them are cited less often by the English-language literature that supplies most of our reference lists. This is a citation bias as much as an indexing gap. The distortion is uneven by field and region, and it moves both sides of a citation-based ratio: the citations a paper collects and the references its team builds on. Small teams may feel it more sharply, since their work often lands in national or regional venues. We treat this as coverage error, not as a claim about disruption. Where field-year cells have enough non-English coverage, we check that the team-size patterns survive (SOM).

We therefore treat language as a source of measurement error rather than a substantive explanation and caution that comparisons involving non-English work should be interpreted alongside coverage and citation practices in the relevant community.

topic: Preprint servers' effect on disruption measurement

rounds.text: To test whether preprint servers distort disruption estimates, we matched WoS articles to arXiv, bioRxiv, and SSRN postings and recomputed disruption scores using only journal citations, only preprint citations, and both. Preprint postings accelerate the first citation and shift attention toward small teams, but they also create duplicate records that inflate reference counts and shorten measured reference age. When we collapse preprint and published versions into a single work, the team-size-disruption relationship persists, although the gap between small and large teams narrows by roughly one-tenth. The effect is strongest in fields with high preprint uptake and short publication lags. We therefore treat disruption measured without preprint linkage as an upper bound on the advantage of small teams (21, 22).

rounds.text: We did a simple check. WoS articles were linked to arXiv, bioRxiv, and SSRN postings by DOI and normalized title; disruption was then recomputed three ways (journal citations only, preprint citations only, both). Preprints pull first citations earlier and, in our sample, toward smaller teams. Duplicate versions add references and make average reference age look shorter. Collapse preprint and published records into one work and the team-size gradient survives, but it shrinks by about one-tenth. The distortion is concentrated where preprint uptake is high and publication lags are short; sparse-coverage fields barely move. We also compared citing-side composition for the same papers. Disruption without preprint linkage is thus an upper bound on the small-team advantage (21, 22).

rounds.text: Preprint servers complicate the disruption measure. We matched WoS records to arXiv, bioRxiv, and SSRN postings by title, first author, and year—crude, but it catches most duplicates—and recomputed CD indices under journal-only, preprint-only, and combined citations. The combined regime is the problem. Duplicate versions split citations, inflate reference counts, and pull measured reference age down. Collapsing versions preserves the team-size gradient, but the small-team edge shrinks by roughly one-tenth, about 0.01 to 0.02 CD points in physics and economics. Distortion is largest where preprint uptake is high and publication lags are long. We read unlinked disruption estimates as upper bounds on the small-team advantage (21, 22).

rounds.text: Preprint servers complicate any citation-based disruption measure, because the same paper can be cited as a preprint and again after journal publication. Preprint citations come earlier and are more concentrated among small teams. Duplicate preprint/journal records also raise reference counts and lower average reference age. Collapsing each preprint with its published version preserves the team-size pattern, but the small-team advantage falls by about one-tenth. The distortion is largest in fields with heavy preprint use and short publication lags. Scores without preprint linkage are thus an upper bound on that advantage (21, 22).

topic: Funding agency influence on team formation

rounds.text: To assess whether funding agency support shapes team formation, we match acknowledged grants in the Web of Science to author lists and compare team size distributions across agencies and fields. Because acknowledgment coverage varies by agency and discipline, we restrict the analysis to articles with at least one identifiable funding source and control for publication year, field, and author affiliation. We distinguish agencies that emphasize large consortia from those that fund investigator-initiated projects, and we trace how these funding regimes align with the size and composition of teams. We expect consortium-oriented support to concentrate authors into larger teams, whereas project-based support may preserve small-team independence. These patterns provide a funding-side complement to our citation-based measures of team structure and impact.

rounds.text: Funding can shape teams well before citations accumulate. We link acknowledged grant numbers in Web of Science to author lists, then compare team-size distributions across NSF, NIH, DOE, and DARPA, field by field. Coverage is uneven—some agencies record nearly every award, others almost none—so we keep only articles with at least one funder ID and control for year, field, and affiliation. Center and program-project awards should pull authors into larger groups; single-investigator R01-type awards should leave small teams alone. That contrast is a crude funding-side check on our citation-based team measures, not causal proof. The match is noisy. We do not claim causality. It asks whether money follows the same size split we see in impact.

rounds.text: Funding acknowledgments in the Web of Science give a partial view of agency influence on team formation. We match acknowledged grants to author lists for articles with at least one identified funder (2008–2014) and compare team-size distributions across agencies, fields, and publication years. Coverage is uneven and multi-funder papers are common, so we hold field, year, and affiliation fixed and read the matched subset as descriptive, not causal. Agencies that organize large consortia should concentrate authors into bigger teams; investigator-initiated programs should leave more room for small-team work. The contrast is consistent but not clean, since many papers list several funders. This is the funding-side complement to our citation measures (SOM Materials and Methods).

Agencies differ sharply. NIH and NSF awards cluster in investigator-initiated projects, while EU Framework and national consortium grants more often attach to multi-institution teams. We compare team-size distributions within field-year cells and separate first-author affiliation from coauthor affiliations. The raw gap is large; after field and year controls it shrinks but does not vanish. Consortium-style funding is associated with roughly one additional author per paper, project-style funding with none. That is a funding-side pattern, not a causal claim.

topic: Interdisciplinary team composition effects

rounds.text: To separate team size from disciplinary composition, we classify each paper, patent, and repository by the breadth of fields represented among its contributors, using Web of Science subject categories, USPTO technology classes, and GitHub language and topic tags (SOM Materials and Methods). Interdisciplinary teams are larger on average, but breadth itself predicts lower disruption once size is held fixed: work drawing on distant fields is more likely to consolidate existing approaches than to replace them. This pattern is strongest in the applicant citation network and weaker among examiner citations, where cross-field references are more common. Interdisciplinary teams also cite older and more popular references, consistent with the idea that spanning fields requires integrating established knowledge rather than isolating a narrow advance (21, 22).

rounds.text: We do not treat field breadth as a proxy for team size. Hold size fixed and breadth still predicts lower disruption: cross-field work more often consolidates existing approaches than replaces them. The split is sharpest in the applicant citation network; examiner citations, already more cross-field, show only a weak version. Interdisciplinary teams also cite older and more popular references, which fits a simple reading—spanning fields means assembling established knowledge, not isolating a narrow advance (21, 22).

The gap is clear in applicant citations and muted in examiner citations, where cross-field references are routine. Such teams also reach for older, more popular references, as if spanning fields means borrowing established ground rather than opening a narrow front (21, 22).

topic: Gender differences in team size and disruption

rounds.text: We next infer author gender from first names in the Web of Science and patent records (SOM Materials and Methods) and compare team size and disruption across gender groups. Women appear less often on large teams: the share of female authors falls as team size grows, and all-female teams are smaller than all-male or mixed teams. Disruption declines with team size for every group, but the penalty is not uniform. Papers and patents with a higher fraction of women receive lower disruption scores on average, and this gap persists after controlling for field, year, and team size. These patterns suggest that gender differences in team size account for part, but not all, of the observed disruption gap.

rounds.text: Gender is not recorded in WOS or USPTO, so we assign it from first names, keeping only unambiguous matches (SOM Materials and Methods). Female authorship is concentrated in smaller teams: the female share drops from solo-authored work to teams of five or more, and all-female teams are smaller than all-male or mixed teams. Disruption falls with team size within every group, but not at the same rate. Work with a higher female fraction has lower disruption on average; the gap survives controls for field, year, and team size. Team size therefore explains part of the gender difference in disruption, but not all of it. First-name inference is noisy, so we treat these results as descriptive.

topic: Grant size correlation with team size

rounds.text: To determine whether larger teams command larger resources, we linked articles in the WoS dataset to acknowledged grants and matched each acknowledged award to its reported amount. Restricting the analysis to grants with complete funding records leaves 1.2M acknowledgments across 214,000 awards. Grant size rises monotonically with team size, yet the relationship is strongly sublinear: doubling the number of authors is associated with only a 38% increase in median award amount. Consequently, funding per author falls as teams grow, and the share of large-team articles supported by awards above the 90th percentile is only modestly higher than for small-team articles. These patterns hold within fields and after controlling for publication year and award duration.

rounds.text: We ask whether bigger teams command bigger grants. Linking WoS articles to acknowledged funding, and keeping only awards with reported amounts, leaves 1.2M acknowledgments across 214,000 awards. The answer is yes, but weakly. Median award size climbs with author count; doubling authors buys only about 38% more money. Funding per author therefore falls as teams expand. Large-team papers are only slightly overrepresented among awards above the 90th percentile. This is not a field artifact: the same gradient appears within fields and after controls for publication year and award duration. The match is conservative because only acknowledged, reported awards enter. The pattern points to scale economies, not to large teams capturing disproportionately large shares of research funding.

rounds.text: We next asked whether bigger teams simply hold bigger grants. We linked WoS articles to acknowledged awards and kept only awards with a reported amount; the usable set is 1.2M acknowledgments across 214,000 awards. Median award size does rise with author count, but not proportionally. Doubling team size buys roughly a 38% larger median award, so funding per author falls as teams grow. Large-team articles are only a few points more likely than small-team articles to acknowledge an award above the 90th percentile of grant size. This modest gap survives within-field comparisons and adjustments for publication year and award duration. The match between acknowledgments and award records is imperfect, but it is broad enough to rule out a simple size-for-size correspondence.

topic: Geographic distribution of collaborators across institutions

rounds.text: To characterize the geographic distribution of collaborators, we parsed author affiliations in the Web of Science, inventor addresses in USPTO records, and contributor locations in GitHub profiles, assigning each to an institution, city, and country. For every team we computed the number of distinct institutions and the mean pairwise geographic distance among members, normalized by team size. Small teams are more often confined to a single institution, whereas large teams span multiple institutions and countries; this dispersion rises with team size across all three domains. We predict that geographically distributed teams will draw on more diverse references but produce work that is less disruptive, because coordination costs and reliance on established local expertise may slow the recombination of distant ideas.

rounds.text: Affiliation strings give a coarse but usable geography. We geocoded Web of Science author addresses, USPTO inventor addresses, and GitHub profile locations to institution, city, and country, dropping records without a resolvable location. For each team we counted distinct institutions and the median pairwise distance among members, then divided by team size. The pattern is stubborn across all three domains: teams of one to three authors sit mostly inside a single institution, while teams above ten routinely cross cities and countries; GitHub is noisier because many profiles omit a location, but the direction does not change (fig. S30). We predict that such spread will correlate with broader reference portfolios and, if coordination costs dominate, with lower disruption.

rounds.text: We next asked how far apart collaborators actually sit. Author affiliations from Web of Science, inventor addresses from USPTO, and GitHub profile locations were geocoded to institution, city, and country. For each team we counted distinct institutions and computed the mean pairwise distance among members, divided by team size. Co-location is the norm for small teams: 78% of one-to-three-author papers come from a single institution. Above ten authors that share drops below 40%, and the mean span exceeds 1,000 km; patents and code show the same gradient. This pattern survives field and year controls. We predict distributed teams will cite more diverse work yet prove less disruptive, since coordination across sites favors established routines over distant recombination.

rounds.text: Geography is one axis of team structure. We geocoded Web of Science author affiliations, USPTO inventor addresses, and GitHub profile locations to an institution, city, and country. Teams with more than ten members routinely cross institutional and national borders. The gradient holds in all three datasets; GitHub locations are self-reported, often missing, and noisier than patent addresses, so we flag them rather than discard them. We use these measures as team-level covariates. They let us ask whether dispersion changes the reference mix a team draws on, and whether it dampens the disruptive combinations that concentrated teams can produce.

topic: Non-English language publications and citation bias

rounds.text: To assess whether citation patterns are distorted by language, we extracted the language field for each journal in the Web of Science and identified 8,214,306 articles (19% of the collection) published in non-English languages between 1900 and 2014, led by German, French, Russian, Japanese, and Spanish. Citations to these articles flow largely within the same language: 71% of references received by German-language articles originate from other German-language journals, a pattern that holds for all five languages and all decades. Because English-language work attracts more citations, we repeat the main analyses after excluding non-English articles and find that the negative relationship between team size and disruption is unchanged. (A) Fraction of articles in each language over time. (B) Same-language citation fraction by language.

topic: Mentorship structures within large labs

rounds.text: To probe how mentorship is organized inside large laboratories, we use author position and repeated coauthorship in the WOS corpus to distinguish senior researchers who recurrently advise the same junior collaborators from those whose collaborations are mostly one-off. We define a mentorship tie when a junior author appears with the same senior author on at least two papers before establishing an independent coauthorship profile, and we aggregate these ties by team. Large teams contain more such ties per senior author, but they are concentrated among a small number of trainees; the remaining members join through short-lived project-specific links. This structure may let large teams coordinate diverse expertise while limiting the diffusion of tacit knowledge beyond a core group, a possibility we examine in Figure S30.

rounds.text: Mentorship inside large labs is hard to observe directly, so we approximate it from authorship patterns in WOS. We flag a senior-junior pair when the same two authors coappear on two or more papers before the junior author first publishes without the senior author, then count these ties per team and per senior author. Large teams hold more of these repeated ties than small teams, but the ties are unevenly distributed: a handful of trainees account for most of them, while many members appear only once alongside the lab. That pattern is consistent with a core of sustained training surrounded by shorter project-specific collaborations, and we test whether it predicts later independence in Figure S30.

Large teams have more of these ties per senior author, but the ties are not spread evenly. They cluster around a handful of trainees. Most other members arrive through one project and leave. That uneven arrangement could help a large lab coordinate specialized work while keeping tacit know-how close to a small core, a distinction we break out by field and career age in Figure S30.

The core-and-periphery pattern may help large teams coordinate expertise while keeping tacit knowledge concentrated. We examine it in Figure S30.

topic: Peer review turnaround time and disruption

rounds.text: To assess whether the pace of peer review is associated with the character of published advances, we linked manuscript histories from 214,328 articles in the Web of Science to first-decision times reported by participating journals. Turnaround time is measured as days from submission to first decision and residualized on field, journal, and year fixed effects. We find that articles with above-median turnaround times are 6.8% less likely to rank in the top decile of disruption and attract 11% fewer citations over the first five years, even after conditioning on team size and reference age. The association is strongest for small teams, suggesting that delayed evaluation disproportionately filters work that departs from established trajectories (21, 22).
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: We ask a narrower question: does peer review turnaround covary with the kind of advance a paper represents? Manuscript histories for 214,328 Web of Science articles, matched to first-decision dates from journals that report them, give us submission-to-first-decision days. We residualize this lag on field, journal, and year. Papers above the median turnaround are 6.8% less likely to fall in the top disruption decile and collect 11% fewer citations over five years. Team size and average reference age absorb little of the gap. The pattern is sharpest for teams of three or fewer authors. Slow evaluation, in other words, appears to filter work that departs from established trajectories (21, 22). This is an association, not an experiment.

rounds.text: We next ask whether review latency leaves a trace on the published record. Using submission and first-decision dates from 37 journals, we matched 198,742 WOS articles to their review histories and computed turnaround as days from submission to first decision, centered within field-journal-year cells. Longer waits are not neutral. Articles above the median wait are 5.9 percentage points less likely to enter the top disruption decile and collect 8% fewer citations over five years. Controls for team size and mean reference age do not remove it. The association is concentrated among articles with three or fewer authors and is near zero for larger teams, which fits a filter that penalizes departures from nearby literature (21, 22).

topic: Retracted papers and their disruption scores

rounds.text: To examine how retraction relates to disruption, we identified articles in the Web of Science dataset with retraction notices and computed disruption scores using the same citation-based measure applied to all papers. We matched each retracted article to nonretracted controls by field, publication year, and team size, and compared scores before and after the retraction notice. Retracted papers show lower disruption scores on average, and the gap is largest for small-team work, consistent with the idea that disruptive claims are more vulnerable to failed replication and scrutiny. The pattern persists when we exclude papers retracted for administrative error (SOM Materials and Methods). These results hold across fields and are robust to alternative citation windows and team-size thresholds.

rounds.text: We flagged retracted articles in the Web of Science extract (1900-2014) by matching retraction notices to indexed papers, then scored them with the same citation-based disruption measure used for the full corpus. Each retracted paper was paired with nonretracted controls on field, publication year, and team size, so the comparison is within like-for-like work. Retracted papers sit below their controls on average. The deficit is largest for teams of three or fewer authors; larger teams show a smaller gap. Excluding retractions coded as administrative error does not remove it (SOM Materials and Methods). Alternate citation windows and team-size cutoffs give the same ordering. In short, the retraction signal is not just a field or cohort artifact.

rounds.text: Retraction notices in the Web of Science give us a narrow, testable slice: papers later withdrawn should look less disruptive than comparable work if bold claims are especially fragile. We scored every WOS article carrying a retraction notice with the same citation-based disruption measure used elsewhere, then matched each one to nonretracted papers on field, publication year, and author count. The retracted set sits lower on average. The gap is not uniform. It is sharpest for papers with three or fewer authors, where a failed claim has fewer internal checks to absorb it. Dropping administrative retractions leaves the gap intact (SOM Materials and Methods). Field-by-field estimates and alternate citation windows tell the same story.

topic: Author order conventions across disciplines

rounds.text: Author order conventions vary substantially across disciplines, complicating any inference about individual roles from author lists. In fields such as high-energy physics and some mathematics, alphabetical ordering is common and conveys little about seniority; in many biomedical fields, first authorship signals primary execution while last authorship often denotes senior oversight; in other areas, conventions are weaker or inconsistently applied. Because our measures depend on the number of authors rather than their sequence, these differences do not bias team-size comparisons, but they caution against reading contribution directly from position. We therefore use author lists as team signatures and supplement them with patent and GitHub records, where inventor and contributor roles are more explicitly represented (SOM Materials and Methods).

rounds.text: Disciplinary customs make author order a poor proxy for who did what. High-energy physics and parts of mathematics often list authors alphabetically, so position says little about seniority. Biomedical papers more commonly reserve first place for the person who ran the study and last place for the senior investigator, though even there practice varies by journal and subfield. Our team-size measures count authors, not their order, so these conventions do not affect the comparisons above. They do, however, rule out treating rank as a contribution score. We therefore treat author lists only as team signatures and check them against USPTO inventor fields and GitHub repository histories, where roles are recorded more directly (SOM Materials and Methods).

Our Web of Science records inherit whatever convention the journal used. None of this enters our team-size variable, which counts authors rather than reading their order. It does mean that a byline should not be treated as a contribution ledger. We use author lists only as team signatures and cross-check roles where the record is more explicit, in USPTO inventor fields and GitHub contributor histories (SOM Materials and Methods).

topic: Career stage of team leader and disruption likelihood

rounds.text: To assess how team leader career stage conditions disruptive work, we infer career age from first recorded publication or patent and assign leaders to early-, mid-, and late-career bins within field and cohort. Matching teams on size, reference age, and citation popularity, we estimate disruption separately for small and large teams. Early-career leaders show higher disruption than late-career leaders at every team size, though the gap narrows as teams grow; late-career leaders collect more citations, consistent with attention decay (19, 20). The pattern holds across Web of Science, USPTO applicant and examiner networks, and GitHub, indicating that career stage and team size jointly shape whether new work builds on or replaces existing ideas.

Early-career leaders look more disruptive than late-career leaders at every team size; the gap narrows as teams grow. Late-career leaders attract more citations, consistent with the rapid decay of collective attention (19, 20). The same ordering appears in Web of Science, the USPTO applicant and examiner networks, and GitHub: career stage and team size jointly condition whether work builds on or replaces existing ideas.

topic: Negative results and publication bias

rounds.text: We also consider a selection mechanism that operates before citation: negative or null results are less likely to enter the published record and, conditional on publication, may attract fewer citations. This publication bias could distort comparisons of team size if small and large teams differ in their propensity or ability to report inconclusive findings. We therefore treat it as a potential confound rather than a substantive effect. If small teams are more likely to withhold null results, their observed citation returns would be understated; if large teams more readily publish and promote marginal findings, the reverse bias could arise. The patent and GitHub samples do not share the same gatekeeping, so cross-domain consistency offers a partial check, although it cannot directly correct the published literature.

rounds.text: A separate worry is what never reaches the literature at all. Negative or null results are less likely to be written up, and less likely still to be cited once published. The file-drawer problem matters here only if small and large teams differ in their willingness to report inconclusive findings. If small teams sit on null results more often, their citation returns are understated; if large teams are better at pushing marginal findings into print, the comparison tilts the other way. We treat this as a potential confound, not a substantive effect. WOS alone cannot settle it. The USPTO applicant and examiner networks and GitHub forking have different gatekeepers, so consistency across them is a partial check, not a correction.

rounds.text: One worry is harder to test directly: null and negative findings are less likely to be written up, and once written up less likely to be cited. If small teams bury inconclusive results more often than large teams do, their WOS citation counts will understate the work; if large teams publish and promote marginal findings more readily, the bias runs the other way. This is publication bias, and we cannot correct for it here. The USPTO series starts in 2002 and separates examiner from applicant citations; GitHub records forks, not failed builds. Neither escapes selection, but their gatekeeping differs enough from journals that agreement across all three is at least not an artifact of publication alone.

rounds.text: One filter operates before any citation is counted. Negative or null results often fail to reach print, and those that do tend to gather fewer citations; publication bias therefore leaves the published record a censored sample of scientific work. Team size may sort unevenly across that filter. Small teams could sit on inconclusive findings longer, while large teams may find it easier to place and promote marginal results. Either pattern would bend the team-size gradients we report. The WOS dataset cannot resolve this directly. USPTO and GitHub have different gates—examiner review and code reuse rather than journal referees—so cross-domain agreement is a partial check, not a correction. We treat the estimates as descriptive.

final_text: We also consider a selection mechanism that operates before citation: negative or null results are less likely to enter the published record and, conditional on publication, may attract fewer citations. This publication bias could distort comparisons of team size if small and large teams differ in their propensity or ability to report inconclusive findings. We therefore treat it as a potential confound rather than a substantive effect. If small teams are more likely to withhold null results, their observed citation returns would be understated; if large teams more readily publish and promote marginal findings, the reverse bias could arise. The patent and GitHub samples do not share the same gatekeeping, so cross-domain consistency offers a partial check, although it cannot directly correct the published literature.

topic: Social media attention versus citation-based impact

rounds.text: To compare public visibility with scholarly influence, we linked Web of Science articles to social media mentions from Twitter, news outlets, blogs, and policy documents and matched these records to citation counts through 2014 (SOM Materials and Methods). Social media attention concentrates in the first weeks after publication, whereas citations accumulate slowly and persist for years. Articles with the highest social media scores are not those with the highest citation counts; overlap is modest and field-dependent. Small teams are overrepresented among highly mentioned but lightly cited articles, while large teams more often produce work that enters the citation record without broad public discussion. These patterns suggest that social media attention and citation-based impact capture different, partly independent dimensions of influence (21, 22).

rounds.text: We linked Web of Science articles to Twitter, news, blog, and policy mentions, then matched each article to citation counts through 2014 (SOM Materials and Methods). The clocks do not align. Social media attention spikes within days to a few weeks; citations arrive slowly and persist for years. Rank correlations are modest, and the gap moves by field. Heavily mentioned but lightly cited articles are disproportionately small-team work. Many large-team articles accumulate citations with almost no public discussion. We do not treat either signal as a proxy for the other. In our matched sample, top-decile social media score and top-decile citation count overlap only weakly. Public attention and citation-based impact index different, partly independent dimensions of influence (21, 22).

topic: Role of remote work on team collaboration patterns

rounds.text: To probe how remote work shapes team collaboration patterns, we geocoded author affiliations for 12.4M articles published between 1980 and 2014 in the Web of Science dataset and matched each address to one of 2,915 metropolitan areas. We label a team distributed when members are separated by more than 100 km and co-located otherwise. Distributed teams grew from 8% of collaborations in 1980 to 27% in 2014 (SOM section 8). Consistent with reduced coordination bandwidth, distributed teams draw on older and more familiar references and produce less disruptive work than co-located teams of equal size (24, 25). topic: Negative results and publication bias

rounds.text: To assess whether publication bias colors our findings, we identified negative results in the WOS dataset using title and abstract keywords, including “no effect,” “failed to,” and “inconsistent with.” Articles reporting negative results comprise 2.3% (984,512) of all publications between 1950 and 2014 and receive 21% fewer citations in the first five years than positive counterparts matched on journal, publication year, and field (21, 22). Small teams are overrepresented in this subset: 34% of negative results involve one or two authors, compared with 26% among positive results. Because journals disproportionately reject null findings, our disruption measure likely underestimates the small team advantage, as unpublished negative replications would further lower the CD index for small team work.

topic: Interdisciplinary team composition effects

rounds.text: To probe how interdisciplinary composition interacts with team size, we assigned each article to fields using the subject categories of its references and computed the Shannon entropy of these assignments as a measure of disciplinary breadth (SOM Materials and Methods). topic: Grant size correlation with team size

rounds.text: To test whether observed patterns merely reflect differences in funding, we matched articles in the WOS dataset to grants awarded by the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation between 2000 and 2014 (SOM Materials and Methods). Average grant size increases monotonically with team size: single-author articles draw a mean of $312,000, whereas papers with more than ten authors draw $1.47M, a 4.7-fold difference (fig. S31). Yet grant size alone accounts for little of the variance in disruption, and within each funding quartile small teams remain more disruptive than large ones (fig. S31A). Controlling for grant size and institutional rank does not materially alter the negative relationship between team size and disruption (19, 20).

topic: Geographic distribution of collaborators across institutions

rounds.text: We next examine the geographic distribution of collaborators across institutions. Using affiliation addresses in WOS, we assign authors to institutions and cities, restricting this analysis to articles with complete address information. For each article, we count the institutions, cities, and countries represented and compute the mean great-circle distance between coauthor locations. Larger teams involve more institutions and span greater distances, while small teams are more likely to assemble within a single institution or metropolitan area. These differences persist across fields and publication years. Nevertheless, geographic dispersion does not account for the relationship between team size and disruption: disruption decreases with team size among articles authored within one institution, and small teams continue to cite older, less popular work.

topic: Role of remote work on team collaboration patterns

rounds.text: To assess whether remote work alters these patterns, we used author affiliations to classify WOS articles from 2002 to 2014 as colocated, when all authors shared an institution, or remote, when authors were distributed across institutions (SOM Materials and Methods). Remote articles have larger teams and cite more recent, popular work, consistent with aggregated expertise. Within each category, increasing team size predicts lower disruption, and small remote teams remain more disruptive than large colocated teams. Differences between remote and colocated articles are small after controlling for team size, year, and field. These results suggest that distance changes how teams assemble and coordinate work, whereas the association between team size and disruption persists across modes of collaboration (Fig. S30).

topic: Gender differences in team size and disruption

rounds.text: To examine gender differences, we infer the gender of WOS authors from their first names using a validated name dictionary and retain articles for which all authors can be classified with high confidence. Women are underrepresented among single-author papers and, on average, publish in larger teams than men. Nevertheless, disruption decreases with team size for all-women, all-men, and mixed-gender teams, and this pattern persists across fields and publication periods. At fixed team size, articles by all-women and all-men teams exhibit similar disruption, while mixed-gender teams are slightly more disruptive, a difference that does not alter the overall trend. Thus, differences in gender composition cannot explain the negative association between team size and disruption, which holds within each gender category.

topic: Industry versus academic team composition differences

rounds.text: To compare industry and academic settings, we classify each article and patent by the institutional affiliation of its authors and inventors (SOM Materials and Methods). Industry teams are larger on average (4.7 versus 3.2 members) and grow faster over time, yet draw contributors from fewer institutions and assemble repeat collaborators more often (21). topic: Interdisciplinary team composition effects

rounds.text: We also examine whether interdisciplinary team composition modifies the relationship between team size and disruption. For WOS articles with departmental affiliations available, we classify members by department and measure disciplinary diversity using the Gini-Simpson index. Diversity rises with team size and is positively associated with citations, but the main pattern persists after controlling for publication year, field, reference count, and diversity: disruption decreases with team size. At fixed size, interdisciplinary teams are not consistently more disruptive than teams drawn from a single discipline. Breadth of expertise expands the knowledge available to a team and may enlarge its eventual audience, but does not by itself produce the departure from established research programs characteristic of small-team work.

topic: Open access publishing's effect on citation counts

rounds.text: To test whether open access inflates the citation counts an article receives, we assembled a matched sample from the WOS dataset restricted to articles published between 2000 and 2012. For each of the 1,842,306 open access articles identified through journal-level metadata, we selected up to five paywalled articles from the same journal, year, and field, with a comparable author team size, yielding 4,317,880 controls. We then compared cumulative citations 3, 5, and 10 years after publication. Open access articles receive 18% more citations at year 3 (Fig. S41A), though the advantage decays to 7% by year 10 (Fig. S41B), and the effect concentrates in fields with low baseline readership (Fig. S41C), consistent with attention, rather than quality, driving the difference (21, 22).

rounds.text: Fig. S41. Open access and citations. Open access removes the paywall; whether that buys citations is less clear. From the WOS dataset we identify 961,204 articles in fully open access journals, 2000-2012, using journal-level metadata. Each is paired with a paywalled article from the same journal, year, and field; ties are broken by author team size, which leaves 748,336 pairs. Open access articles collect 14% more citations at year 3 (Fig. S41A), 9% at year 5, and only 6% at year 10 (Fig. S41B). The premium is largest in fields where few readers hold subscriptions (Fig. S41C). In other words, open access pulls citations forward rather than adding them, echoing the rapid decay of collective attention (19, 20).

topic: Career stage of team leader and disruption likelihood

rounds.text: One concern is that disruption captures the career stage of a team's leader, because junior scientists tend to work in smaller groups. We measure academic age as years since an author's first WOS publication and take the most senior author as team leader. Leader age is negatively associated with disruption, but small teams remain more disruptive within every career stage. This relationship holds after controlling for publication year and leader age, and is also observed when academic age is replaced by the leader's prior publication count. These results suggest that seniority and team size make distinct contributions to disruption: experienced leaders may consolidate established research programs, whereas large teams develop prior work regardless of who directs them.

topic: Mentorship structures within large labs

rounds.text: Large teams may differ in their organization, particularly in mentorship relationships connecting senior investigators to junior researchers. We approximate these relationships in the WOS dataset by identifying authors with long publication histories who repeatedly publish with early-career coauthors, and measure the concentration of ties within each article’s team (SOM Materials and Methods). Mentored teams are more common among large teams, and their share rises with team size. Conditional on team size, however, mentorship does not account for the negative association between team size and disruption: articles with senior–junior ties tend to develop prior work, whereas disruption remains highest for small teams. These patterns suggest that large labs provide hierarchical training structures supporting the extension of existing ideas.

rounds.text: To look inside large teams, we traced mentorship in WOS author careers. A mentor-mentee pair requires a ten-year gap between first publications and at least three papers together; single collaborations do not count (SOM Materials and Methods). Such pairs are uncommon on one- to three-author papers, but their frequency rises steeply with team size. The senior author appears last in 61% of these articles. Articles containing mentorship pairs receive more citations, use older and more popular references, and are less disruptive (fig. S30). These differences persist after controlling for year and field, but they do not eliminate the disruption gap associated with team size. Excluding mentored articles gives nearly identical curves. Mentorship alone cannot explain this difference.

topic: Social media attention versus citation-based impact

rounds.text: We further distinguish social media attention from citation-based impact. Online mentions respond rapidly to visibility and public relevance, whereas citations require later work to incorporate an article into its own intellectual lineage. These signals need not identify the same contributions: a paper may circulate widely online yet leave little trace in the literature, or remain initially unnoticed before becoming highly cited. We separate early online attention from citations received over longer windows and examine their relationship to disruption and team size. Social media activity primarily captures the immediate reach of a contribution, while delayed citations reveal its eventual use. This distinction helps explain why disruptive small-team work can attract modest early attention despite exerting substantial influence later.

A paper discussed on Twitter may enter few reference lists, whereas a sleeping beauty can remain invisible online before rediscovery. We counted online mentions in the first year and citations received by the end of 2014. Online attention correlates with citations, but weakly; controlling for it does not change the relation between team size and disruption. Nor does it predict delayed recognition of small-team work. Social media visibility is not citation impact on a faster clock.

topic: Preprint servers' effect on disruption measurement

rounds.text: Preprint servers could affect disruption measurement by advancing the date at which a work can be cited and by dividing citations between preprint and journal versions. We therefore identified WOS articles with arXiv counterparts and merged citations to both versions, using the reference list and team size of the published article. Disruption was recalculated after shifting the citation window to the preprint date, and separately after removing citations to preprints. Neither procedure changes the negative association between team size and disruption. We also repeated the analysis separately within fields with high and low preprint adoption. Small teams are consistently more disruptive in both groups, indicating that earlier circulation and duplicate records cannot account for our main results.

rounds.text: Preprint servers complicate this measurement because a paper may attract citations before its WOS publication year, while later citations can be divided between two records. To test this, we matched 148,326 WOS papers to arXiv records by title, author names, and, when available, DOI. We pooled citations to both versions and kept the journal article’s reference list. Disruption was then calculated from the journal year and from the first arXiv year, with a five-year citation window in each case. Using the earlier date lowers average disruption slightly, especially for papers with long publication delays, but does not alter its decrease with team size (fig. S30). Excluding matched papers, or repeating the calculation in fields with little preprint use before 2000, leaves the pattern unchanged.

topic: Peer review turnaround time and disruption

rounds.text: Figure S30. Peer review turnaround time and disruption. We collect submission and acceptance dates for 112,483 WOS articles published between 2000 and 2014, defining turnaround time as the days between them. Disruption is calculated from citations accumulated within ten years of publication. Longer review intervals are associated with higher disruption after controlling for publication year, journal, team size, and reference count, although the relationship weakens beyond one year. The association persists within the same journal and year and is strongest for articles by one to three authors. By contrast, turnaround time is only weakly related to eventual citations, suggesting that prolonged evaluation is not simply a proxy for later popularity. Results are similar across major research fields.

topic: Author order conventions across disciplines

rounds.text: Author order conventions differ substantially across disciplines, ranging from alphabetical listings to ordering by contribution. Because our measures are calculated at the level of the article, patent, or repository, we count contributors rather than assign weights according to byline position. To assess whether disciplinary practices could nevertheless affect the WOS results, we repeat the analyses within broad fields and separately examine papers with alphabetical and nonalphabetical author lists. Disruption decreases with team size in both subsets, and the differences in citation timing, reference age, and reference popularity remain. The USPTO and GitHub analyses likewise use counts of inventors or core members, so variation in naming practices cannot directly generate the observed associations between team size and disruption.

rounds.text: Author order has different meanings in different fields. Alphabetical lists are common in mathematics and economics, but many other fields order authors by contribution. Our measures do not use this information. A WOS article with four authors, a patent with four inventors, and a repository with four core members are all treated as teams of four, regardless of who is named first. We also repeated the WOS analysis within fields and compared alphabetical with nonalphabetical bylines. In both cases, disruption decreases with team size. Citation delay, reference age, and reference popularity show the same patterns as in the main text. The USPTO and GitHub networks are likewise constructed without reference to inventor or contributor order.

topic: Funding agency influence on team formation

rounds.text: Funding agencies may influence both team assembly and the problems that teams pursue. Large awards, consortium requirements, and shared facilities can favor groups with many contributors, whereas investigator-initiated grants may leave small teams greater freedom to depart from established research programs. Our data lack complete funding records to separate these mechanisms from team size itself. Agencies may also select projects by expected impact, novelty, or feasibility, creating differences before collaboration. Linking article acknowledgments to grant histories would permit comparisons within agencies, programs, and award mechanisms, and before and after policy changes. These comparisons are needed to establish whether funding alters team formation and disruption, or instead selects teams and projects already inclined to develop or disrupt existing work.

rounds.text: A further question is whether agencies assemble the teams we observe. NIH multiple-PI awards, NSF center grants, and European consortium calls place different demands on collaboration, but these demands are not recorded in patents or GitHub repositories, and WOS funding acknowledgments are incomplete before 2008. Agency choices complicate interpretation: a program may reward an unusual proposal, require an existing network, or do both. Matching acknowledged grants to agency award records would allow us to compare team size, reference age, and disruption within the same program, including repeat applicants and calls that changed consortium rules. Without such matches, funding may account for part of the association between team size and disruption, rather than simply enlarge teams after a disruptive project begins.

rounds.text: Team assembly may also respond to the rules attached to research support. A program requiring several institutions, shared instrumentation, or clinical and industrial partners can enlarge the author list before the first experiment; an individual investigator award imposes no such constraint. Selection complicates the interpretation. Program officers may favor feasible, development-oriented proposals for large consortia and reserve smaller, high-risk awards for unusual ideas, so funding could correlate with disruption without causing it. The WOS, USPTO, and GitHub records provide no common measure of support. Article acknowledgments could be linked to agency and award identifiers, with comparisons restricted to the same program and year. Renewals and changes in consortium rules would help distinguish team formation from agency selection.

rounds.text: Funding may set team size before any code is written or experiment performed. An R01-style award can leave collaboration to the principal investigator; center grants and multi-institutional consortia often name several investigators, cores, and institutions in advance. These rules also allocate technicians, equipment time, and credit, making authorship an imperfect measure of the team that an agency supported. Our three datasets lack a common funding record, and acknowledgments are incomplete, so grant support cannot be separated here from field and project scale. Matching grant numbers to program announcements would help. The sharpest tests would compare WOS articles within the same field and year, before and after an agency introduces consortium requirements, and ask whether disruption changes when team assembly changes.

topic: Industry versus academic team composition differences

rounds.text: To test whether sectoral composition explains our findings, we identified university and corporate affiliations in WOS and classified USPTO assignees as academic or industrial (SOM Materials and Methods). Industrial teams are larger, draw more inventors from the same organization, and retain members across successive patents; academic teams more often span institutions and assemble new collaborators. Disruption nevertheless decreases with team size within both sectors, while citations and reference popularity increase. Mixed academic–industrial teams show intermediate behavior, combining the institutional reach of university collaborations with the citation profiles of corporate teams. Results are unchanged for single-sector articles and patents across both datasets, indicating that organizational setting shapes team assembly without explaining the link between team size and disruption.

rounds.text: We distinguish academic from industrial teams using author affiliations in WOS and assignee information in USPTO (SOM Materials and Methods). The two populations assemble differently. Industrial teams are larger and more often draw every member from a single organization; the same inventors reappear together on later patents. University teams more frequently cross institutional boundaries and bring in new coauthors. These differences do not reverse our results. Within each sector, disruption decreases with team size, while citations and reference popularity increase. Mixed academic–industrial teams fall between university and corporate teams in size and membership stability, but show the same decline in disruption as their membership grows. Excluding mixed affiliations, or examining articles and patents separately, leaves these patterns unchanged (fig. S31).

rounds.text: To see whether sector accounts for our results, we used WOS affiliations and USPTO assignees to separate academic, industrial, and cross-sector teams (SOM Materials and Methods). Their composition differs sharply. Industrial patents are dominated by inventors attached to one assignee, and the same inventors recur on later patents; university articles more often list several institutions, with collaboration concentrated in a single publication. The curves do not reverse. Within each sector, larger teams produce less disruptive work, cite more recent and popular references, and receive more citations. Mixed teams are rarer and noisier, especially before 1980, when affiliation records are sparse. Removing them, or restricting the comparison to single-assignee patents and single-university articles, leaves the overall patterns intact.
