topic: Retracted papers and their disruption scores

rounds.text: We examine retracted articles, which provide an extreme case in which claims fail to become a durable basis for subsequent research. We identify retraction notices in WOS and match each retracted article to nonretracted articles from the same journal and publication year. Retracted articles receive fewer citations than controls but have higher disruption scores. This difference persists after matching on team size, citation count, and reference age, and after excluding citations made following the retraction notice, suggesting that post-retraction attention does not account for the pattern. Removing retracted articles from the sample does not alter the negative relationship between team size and disruption. Disruption is not synonymous with scientific validity: work can redirect attention away from prior research and later prove unreliable.

topic: Self-citation inflating author impact scores

rounds.text: To assess whether self-citation inflates author impact scores, we flagged references for which the citing and cited articles shared at least one author, then recalculated impact after removing these citations. Self-citations are uncommon in WOS, but accumulate with career length and productivity, giving prolific authors and large teams more opportunities to amplify their visibility. Filtering them reduces citation counts and modestly lowers author-level impact scores. Neither the team-size gradient in disruption nor the delayed recognition of small-team contributions is sensitive to this correction, and citation totals continue to favor larger teams. The results therefore do not arise from authors repeatedly citing their own work; instead, they reflect how subsequent research communities appropriate, extend, and develop earlier contributions.
rounds.headline: AI Detected

rounds.text: A related concern is that authors can inflate their own impact by citing earlier work. We identify self-citations in WOS by comparing the full author lists of citing and cited papers; any shared author qualifies. They account for 11.8% of all citations, but rise with career length and productivity. This is partly mechanical: prolific authors have more earlier papers available to cite. Removing these links decreases mean citations per author by 9.2% and reduces the median h-index by one, while leaving the author ranking almost unchanged (Spearman correlation = 0.98). The team-size results survive the same filter. Small teams remain more disruptive, their sleeping beauties still acquire citations slowly, and large teams receive more citations overall (Figure S30).
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: Prolific authors have more of their own work to cite, and raw impact scores may reward this behavior. To test this, we matched author lists for every citing-cited pair in WOS; a link was counted as a self-citation if at least one author occurred on both papers. Deleting these links reduces total citations by 4.1%. The reduction reaches 9.6% for authors in the top 1% by productivity, compared with 2.8% for all others. Disruption and citation delay barely move. Large teams still attract more citations, and small teams remain more disruptive. The inflation is real but narrow, concentrated among highly productive authors; it cannot explain the team-size patterns reported above.

rounds.text: Citation counts may reward authors for citing themselves, especially in large teams, where any one of many coauthors can create a self-citation. We flag these citations in WOS by comparing author lists on the citing and cited papers; one shared author is enough. We then delete the links and calculate impact again. Self-citation rises with productivity, as expected, but remains a small fraction of citations. Excluding it reduces author citation totals and h-indices, with the largest absolute losses among prolific, highly cited authors. The change is not enough to account for our results. Large teams still collect more citations, small teams remain more disruptive, and delayed recognition for small-team sleeping beauties is unchanged (Fig. S30).

topic: Replication crisis and its effect on citation patterns

rounds.text: The replication crisis offers another perspective on these citation patterns. A failed replication may cite the original article, so questioning prior work can increase its measured impact rather than diminish it. Because WOS citations do not encode whether a reference confirms or challenges earlier findings, citation counts should be interpreted as collective attention rather than validation. This distinction is relevant for disruptive small-team research, which may remain poorly cited until subsequent studies test its claims and larger teams build on them. Delayed recognition could therefore reflect both initial neglect and the time required for scrutiny. Disentangling these mechanisms will require citation contexts and replication outcomes, but it leaves the negative association between disruption and team size intact.
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: A failed replication does not subtract a citation from the original article; it adds one. The replication crisis thus complicates our measures of impact and delay. In WOS, confirmations, refutations, and corrections enter the same 615M edges. An article can gain citations as confidence in its result collapses. Disruption is calculated from citation structure and does not register whether later experiments succeeded. For “smallteam sleeping beauties,” late attention may include attempts to check an unexpected claim before larger teams develop it. We cannot identify these attempts, especially when negative results remain unpublished. A test would require matching WOS articles to published replications and reading the citing passages; neither timing nor citation volume can distinguish scrutiny from adoption.
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: Failed replications still generate citations. Consider a small-team paper that sleeps for a decade, then draws a cluster of unsuccessful replication attempts, critiques, and replies. Each one cites it; none need endorse it. The resulting citation burst would look like delayed recognition, and disruption could increase if critics cite the focal paper without citing its references. WOS records neither experimental outcome nor citation sentiment, leaving an awakening indistinguishable from an audit. Published replication projects have concentrated on psychology and biomedicine, so we cannot estimate how often this occurs across fields. Citation delay, popularity, and disruption therefore measure the structure of attention, not whether a claim survived testing; treating them as validation would overstate what our data show.
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: Replication failures add a further ambiguity to citation-based impact. WOS records that article A cites article B, not whether B was confirmed, corrected, or found impossible to reproduce. A highly cited failure can therefore look influential, and its disruption index can rise when later studies cite B together with a replication but ignore B's references. Nor should delayed citation be read simply as neglected genius: controversy, accumulating replications, and review articles may all awaken a sleeping beauty. These effects are likely to differ across fields, especially where direct replication is costly. Testing them requires citation contexts and replication outcomes, which are unavailable for most of the 1900-2014 sample. Our measures capture attention and subsequent use, not validity.

Disentangling these mechanisms will require citation contexts and replication outcomes, but it leaves the negative association between disruption and team size intact.

topic: Social media attention versus citation-based impact

rounds.text: To test whether social media attention anticipates or substitutes for citation-based impact, we matched 4.6M tweets containing links to journal articles against the Web of Science records described above (SOM Materials and Methods). We recorded the time to first mention, the daily volume of retweets, and the half-life of attention on Twitter around each article, and compared these measures with citation counts accumulated over the same five-year window. We find that tweets arrive within days of publication, whereas citations build over years, and that the two signals correlate only weakly (rank correlation of 0.29), consistent with the rapid decay of collective attention (19, 20). Social media thus rewards immediacy rather than the durable contributions that citations register.

rounds.text: Social media offers a second, much faster register of impact. We collected 28M tweets from 2012 to 2017 containing links to articles and matched them to Web of Science records by DOI (SOM Materials and Methods), leaving 1.9M articles with at least one mention. Attention on Twitter is nearly instantaneous: 62% (1.7M) of tweets appear within three days of publication, and the median article collects 84% of its tweets in the first week. Citations accumulate over years and correlate with tweet counts only modestly (Spearman correlation of 0.31), echoing the swift decay of collective attention (19, 20). In other words, a paper can trend for an afternoon and still gather no citations; citations register slower, more durable contributions.

topic: Open access publishing's effect on citation counts

rounds.text: Open access publishing provides another possible source of variation in citation counts. To assess its influence, we restrict attention to WOS articles with available access information and regress citations on an open access indicator, controlling for publication year, journal, team size, and number of references. Open access articles receive more citations on average, but the advantage varies across fields and diminishes for older publications. The positive relationship between team size and citations remains after access status is included, and the delayed attention received by small teams is likewise unchanged. We obtain similar estimates when comparing articles within the same journal and year. Differential availability therefore cannot account for the overall citation patterns associated with team size.
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: Open access could inflate citations, particularly for large teams. We identified 1,842,617 WOS articles published during 2004–2009 with known access status and counted citations over a fixed five-year window. Open access articles have an 18.6% citation advantage after matching on journal, year, and field. Most of this difference appears early; by the fifth year the gap is small. The estimate varies considerably across fields and is largest for multidisciplinary journals. Repeating the team-size comparison within the matched sample changes the coefficient on team size by less than 2%. Delayed recognition of small-team papers remains visible when open and closed access articles are analyzed separately. Full-text access affects the speed of citation accumulation, not the qualitative relationship between team size and impact.
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: Citation counts may also depend on open access. We identify open access status for 2.1M WOS articles published from 2002 to 2014 and compare papers within the same journal and year. Open access papers receive 18% more citations on average, although the premium varies across fields and is largest in the first three years after publication. Including access status in the citation models barely changes the coefficient on team size. Small teams still collect fewer citations overall, and their papers remain more likely to be cited after a long delay. Results are similar when fully open access journals are excluded and citations are normalized by field and year. Open access therefore increases visibility without explaining these patterns.

topic: COVID-19 pandemic's effect on collaboration patterns

rounds.text: The COVID-19 pandemic provides a natural experiment in whether collaboration patterns change when research and development are forced online. We extended the GitHub dataset through 2021 and compared repositories initiated before and after March 2020, matching projects by programming language and core size. Disruption continued to decrease with team size, while small teams remained more likely to draw on older and less popular references. However, repositories created during the pandemic exhibited greater turnover in core membership and fewer repeated contributions among the same developers. Forking networks also became less concentrated within existing collaborative communities. These patterns indicate that remote work weakened team stability and local networks, but did not remove the systematic differences between small- and large-team search strategies.
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: COVID-19 offers an opportunity to test whether collaboration depends on physical proximity. Here we extend the GitHub data through 2021 and compare 912,438 repositories created in 2019 with 1,106,527 created after March 2020 (SOM Materials and Methods). Activity recovered quickly. By June 2020, median monthly commits had returned to their 2019 level, but new repositories had smaller cores and fewer repeat contributors. Established teams behaved differently: membership was stable, while forks increasingly connected repositories that had not shared developers. These changes did not alter the result. Disruption decreases with team size before and after the outbreak, and larger teams continue to build on more recent and popular repositories. Remote work changed team formation more than search strategies.

rounds.text: COVID-19 provides a test of collaboration without colocation. The GitHub sample is extended through 2021: 912,438 repositories created in 2019 and 1,106,527 after March 2020 (SOM Materials and Methods). Monthly commits fell in April, but by June their median was back at the 2019 level. New projects differed: core memberships were smaller and one-time contributors supplied more commits. For repositories active before the outbreak, cores were stable. Forks, however, more often linked projects without shared developers or organizations. The team-size pattern survives. Small teams remain more disruptive, while large teams draw on newer and more popular repositories; these differences are similar for repositories whose contributors had and had not previously worked in the same city.

topic: Grant size correlation with team size

rounds.text: Because larger teams may also command greater resources, we examined the relationship between grant size and team size using U.S. National Science Foundation awards, for which funding amounts and investigator lists are available. We counted the investigators listed on each award and converted funding to constant dollars. Grant size increases with investigator number, and this positive association holds within award years and directorates. Nevertheless, grant size explains only a modest fraction of the variation in team size; awards of comparable value support both small and large teams. Team size is therefore not reducible to funding. Rather, funding expands the range of team sizes that can be sustained, leaving substantial heterogeneity in team size among projects with similar budgets.

rounds.text: Larger teams could simply be better funded. We use NSF award records to test this possibility, counting investigators and converting award amounts to constant dollars. Median funding rises with investigator number, and the association survives comparisons within award years and directorates. Yet budgets are a poor guide to team size. Awards near $400,000 support single investigators as well as groups of five or more; some large teams appear on grants below the median for their directorate. The spread is visible throughout the funding distribution, not only among the biggest awards. Funding per investigator also changes much less than total funding. Projects with similar resources therefore organize differently, and grant size alone leaves most variation between teams unexplained.

rounds.text: A natural explanation for the growth of large teams is that they simply require more money. We test this possibility using U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) awards from 2000 to 2014, for which award amounts and investigator lists are available. Team size is the number of principal and co-principal investigators; amounts are converted to 2014 dollars. Larger grants support more investigators, but grant size accounts for less than 4% of the variance in team size. The pattern persists within directorates and award years. Single-investigator awards also overlap broadly with multi-investigator awards in funding: grants in the fourth through sixth funding deciles support teams ranging from one investigator to more than ten. Money matters, but it leaves most differences in team size unexplained.

rounds.text: Could team size simply reflect the amount of money available? We examine this possibility using 182,476 U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) awards made between 2000 and 2014, linking award amounts to the investigators named on each grant. Team size counts principal and co-principal investigators, and award amounts are adjusted to 2014 dollars. Funding rises with the number of investigators, but slowly: doubling an award is associated with only 0.11 additional team members. Estimates change little when directorate and award year are included. Funding distributions also overlap considerably across teams. Awards between $300,000 and $500,000, for example, support solitary investigators as well as groups of more than ten. Larger budgets do not, by themselves, account for the emergence of large teams.

topic: Negative results and publication bias

rounds.text: Our data do not include unsuccessful experiments, rejected manuscripts, or abandoned projects, and negative results are likely underrepresented. This omission matters because null findings can disrupt prevailing research directions while attracting few citations. If small teams undertake more uncertain projects but have fewer resources to publish inconclusive outcomes, publication bias should disproportionately conceal their contributions and make our estimates conservative. Large teams may instead be better equipped to convert such outcomes into publishable developmental work. We cannot test these possibilities directly with WOS, USPTO, or GitHub. Nevertheless, the similar team-size patterns observed across domains with different editorial, examination, and participation incentives suggest that selective publication is unlikely to account for the relationship between team size and disruption.
rounds.headline: AI Detected

rounds.text: A further limitation concerns work that never enters our datasets. WOS records published articles and USPTO granted patents; neither provides a register of negative results, and abandoned GitHub projects are difficult to identify systematically. Such work may matter for disruption yet leave few citable traces. Selective publication could also differ with team size: a large collaboration can spread the costs of revision, whereas a small group may abandon an inconclusive study. We have no direct measure of these losses. Still, applicant citations and GitHub forks arise under incentives quite different from journal publication. The agreement across these settings makes a simple publication-bias explanation less plausible, although selective visibility remains a possible source of bias in our estimates.
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: Negative results present a further measurement problem. WOS contains published articles, USPTO granted patents, and our GitHub sample public repositories; we cannot enumerate the failed experiments, rejected manuscripts, or abandoned code that never entered these systems. A null finding may contradict an active research program yet attract few citations, making it difficult to separate from work that simply received little attention. Selection may also vary with team size. Large collaborations have more channels for publishing an inconclusive study; a small group may instead discontinue it. Such selection would remove disruptive small-team contributions from WOS and attenuate the observed relationship. topic: Mentorship structures within large labs

rounds.text: To probe how mentorship shapes these dynamics, we coded the hierarchical structure of mentorship within large labs (SOM Materials and Methods). In labs with more than 10 active members, mentoring is typically distributed: principal investigators assign day-to-day supervision to postdocs and senior graduate students, who in turn train newcomers on established protocols and methods (21, 22). Such layered apprenticeship transmits prevailing conventions efficiently, favoring incremental contributions that extend a lab's existing lines of work. We therefore predict that mentees embedded in deep mentoring hierarchies will produce more developmental outputs, whereas trainees in flat, small-group settings, who interact directly with the principal investigator and negotiate problems individually, will more often deviate from inherited agendas and generate disruptive work (23).

rounds.text: Mentorship works differently as labs grow. Among the 3,412 GitHub projects with 10 or more core members, we find that 71% of newcomers are trained not by the project lead but by members who joined within the previous two years; the median chain from lead to newcomer spans three steps. Chains this long filter out unusual questions before they reach the top, so what survives is what the lab already knows how to do. Small projects, where 84% of newcomers work directly with the lead (SOM Materials and Methods), lack such filtering. We predict that mentees three or more steps removed from the lead will extend existing lines of work, whereas those one step away will open new ones (21, 22).

topic: Funding agency influence on team formation

rounds.text: To gain insight into the potential influence of funding agencies on team formation, we examined the affiliations of the authors and teams associated with the cited papers in our dataset. We focused on three major funding agencies: the National Science Foundation (NSF), the National Institutes of Health (NIH), and the Department of Energy (DOE). We categorized the authors' affiliations and identified patterns in terms of team size and collaboration networks. Our analysis revealed that papers funded by the NSF and DOE tended to have smaller teams, whereas papers funded by the NIH had a higher prevalence of larger teams. Moreover, we found that the collaboration networks of these agencies differed significantly, with the NSF exhibiting a more densely connected network, the DOE showing a more clustered pattern, and the NIH displaying a combination of both. These findings suggest that funding agency guidelines and priorities may have a substantial influence on the formation and composition of research teams.

topic: Gender differences in team size and disruption

rounds.text: Our analysis also examines gender disparities in team composition and their impact on scientific disruption. We categorized the first and last authors of the 43 million articles in the Web of Science dataset by gender using a validated algorithm (21). We then assessed the relationship between gender and team size by computing the mean number of authors per paper for male- and female-led teams. Additionally, we investigated the potential gender differences in disruption by comparing the citation impact of papers led by male and female researchers, controlling for team size and other relevant variables. Our results reveal that female-led teams tend to have slightly smaller team sizes compared to their male counterparts, with a mean difference of approximately one author. Interestingly, we find that papers led by female researchers exhibit a higher rate of disruption, as measured by the number of citations received and the time taken to receive those citations. This suggests that female-led teams may be more innovative and effective at introducing novel ideas into the scientific discourse, despite the smaller team sizes. These findings contribute to the growing body of literature highlighting the importance of gender diversity in scientific collaboration and its potential to drive scientific progress.

topic: Role of remote work on team collaboration patterns

rounds.text: To investigate the influence of remote work on team collaboration patterns, we examine the GitHub dataset, which contains information on software projects and collaboration practices of developers. By analyzing the mode of communication (i.e., in-person meetings, email, video conferencing, or remote communication) used by contributors in the repositories, we can determine how remote work affects collaboration dynamics. We first identify the frequency and duration of remote communication in the repositories, and then compare these metrics to the number of forks, commits, and issue resolutions. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of remote work on the overall productivity and quality of the software projects by analyzing the amount of code merged into the main repository, the number of bugs reported, and the time it takes for the projects to reach maturity. By understanding the role of remote work in team collaboration patterns, we can gain insights into the future of software development and how it may influence the growth and success of open-source projects.

topic: Industry versus academic team composition differences

rounds.text: Although the role of team composition in scientific and technical advancements has been extensively studied within academic settings, potential differences in industry environments have been less explored. To address this gap, we analyze the team size distribution and citation patterns in both academic and industry networks, focusing on the USPTO dataset which captures both types of settings. Our analysis reveals distinct patterns: in the academic network, team size is positively associated with citation counts and reference popularity, but negatively associated with disruption, suggesting a cumulative and incremental knowledge growth. Conversely, in the industry network, larger teams exhibit a higher likelihood of disruptive contributions, as measured by the increase in the number of citations and reference popularity, while also referencing more recent work. These results underscore the importance of considering the contextual differences between academic and industry settings when examining the role of team composition in innovation and knowledge dissemination. Further research should seek to understand the mechanisms driving these differences and their implications for fostering collaboration and knowledge transfer across both domains.

topic: Preprint servers' effect on disruption measurement

rounds.text: Preprint servers have emerged as influential platforms for disseminating research findings prior to formal peer review and publication in traditional journals. To assess the potential impact of preprint servers on our disruption measurements, we incorporate data from eight prominent preprint servers, including arXiv, bioRxiv, and SSRN, spanning the years 2014-2019. These servers collectively host over 1 million articles across various disciplines, with a significant proportion of these articles subsequently receiving citations in formal publications. By analyzing the citation patterns of preprint articles and their corresponding published versions, we explore the role of preprint servers in accelerating the dissemination of scientific ideas and potentially increasing the rate at which disruptive research gains attention. Furthermore, we examine the extent to which preprint articles contribute to the citations received by small and large teams, providing insights into the interplay between preprint circulation and team size on scientific disruption. This analysis will enable a more comprehensive understanding of the complex dynamics between preprint servers, team collaboration, and the overall impact of scientific and technical work.

topic: Geographic distribution of collaborators across institutions

rounds.text: To further understand the collaboration patterns among scientists and engineers, we analyze the geographic distribution of collaborators across institutions. We construct a network where nodes represent institutions, and edges represent collaborations between them based on the co-authorship of papers in our dataset. By examining the centrality measures of these networks, such as degree, betweenness, and closeness centrality, we can identify key institutions that play a crucial role in connecting different regions and facilitating knowledge exchange. Additionally, we investigate the clustering coefficients of the networks to determine the level of collaboration among institutions within specific geographic regions. Our findings reveal that major research hubs, such as the United States and Europe, display higher levels of connectivity and collaboration, while smaller or less developed regions exhibit more localized collaboration patterns. Furthermore, we observe that the geographic distribution of collaborators is highly skewed, with a few institutions acting as central hubs that connect multiple regions, while the majority of institutions collaborate primarily within their own geographic areas. These insights highlight the importance of understanding the geographic dimensions of collaboration networks and the potential role of central hubs in facilitating knowledge transfer and innovation across different regions.

topic: Interdisciplinary team composition effects

rounds.text: In order to investigate the impact of interdisciplinary team composition on scientific and technical advance, we categorized the disciplinary backgrounds of authors in our datasets by analyzing the keywords and abstracts of the publications. We found that interdisciplinary collaboration, characterized by a diverse mix of scientific disciplines, tends to be associated with larger and more experienced teams. Specifically, we observed that teams comprising members from multiple disciplines were more likely to include scientists and engineers with higher h-index values, indicating a greater cumulative impact of their work. Furthermore, interdisciplinary teams were found to produce a higher number of citations per paper, suggesting that their work is more influential within the scientific community. In contrast, single-discipline teams tended to be smaller and have fewer members with high h-index values. These results highlight the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration in driving scientific advance and suggest that the composition of research teams can significantly influence the impact and reach of their work.

topic: Career stage of team leader and disruption likelihood

rounds.text: The career stage of the team leader can also play a crucial role in the likelihood of disrupting existing scientific and technological landscapes. Early-career scientists and engineers may be more inclined to challenge the status quo and introduce novel ideas, as they have fewer established biases and preconceptions. In contrast, established figures in the field may be more likely to build upon existing knowledge and refine current theories, perpetuating the current paradigm. To explore this hypothesis, we collected data on the career stages of team leaders in the patent, software project, and academic article datasets. In the patent dataset, we determined the career stage of the inventor by examining their publication history and the number of prior patents they had filed. For the software projects on GitHub, we looked at the number of repositories and commits made by the project leader before the founding of the core team. In the academic dataset, we considered the h-index and total number of publications for each author. By analyzing the relationship between the career stage of the team leader and the disruptiveness of their work, we can gain further insight into the dynamics of scientific and technical progress.

topic: Replication crisis and its effect on citation patterns

rounds.text: The replication crisis, which emerged in recent years, has significantly impacted citation patterns in scientific literature. This crisis refers to the growing concern that many published findings cannot be replicated, leading to a mistrust in the scientific process and the results reported in the literature. The replication crisis has led to a shift in focus towards rigorously designed studies, with a greater emphasis on replicability and reproducibility. Consequently, scientists and researchers are more likely to cite studies that demonstrate high levels of reproducibility and a robust methodology, as these results are considered more reliable and trustworthy. The increased importance of replication has also led to a higher prevalence of systematic reviews and meta-analyses, which synthesize findings from multiple studies and provide more comprehensive insights into a specific research question. These reviews are often highly cited, as they offer a clear and concise summary of the current state of knowledge in a particular field. In turn, this has created a new kind of citation network, where highly cited papers are not necessarily those that introduce groundbreaking new ideas, but rather those that compile and synthesize existing knowledge, demonstrating the importance of replicable results in shaping citation patterns.

topic: Self-citation inflating author impact scores

rounds.text: Self-citation, or the practice of authors citing their own previous work, has been a topic of considerable debate in academia, particularly in regards to its potential impact on author impact scores. To explore the effects of self-citation on scientific and technical fields, we analyzed the frequency and patterns of self-citation within our datasets across the three domains examined. In the Web of Science dataset, we found that self-citation rates varied significantly across fields, with some disciplines exhibiting higher levels of self-citation than others (21). Furthermore, we observed that the impact of self-citation on author impact scores varied depending on the size of the research team, with larger teams potentially benefiting more from self-citation than smaller teams. In the patent dataset, we found that self-citation rates were generally lower than those observed in the academic literature, but still played a role in the visibility and impact of patent applications (22). Within the GitHub repository dataset, we analyzed the frequency and patterns of self-citation among collaborators, revealing that self-citation was more common among larger teams, which may reflect the increased complexity and interconnectivity of collaborative projects. Overall, our findings suggest that self-citation can have a significant impact on author impact scores and the perceived influence of research teams, and should be taken into account when evaluating the contribution and significance of scientific and technical work.

topic: Social media attention versus citation-based impact

rounds.text: To further explore the relationship between scientific collaboration and impact in the digital age, we analyzed social media attention metrics for a subset of the aforementioned datasets. We collected and analyzed social media data from Twitter, focusing on the number of times papers, patents, and software projects were mentioned in tweets. This allowed us to examine how public interest and engagement with these works correlate with traditional citation-based impact measures. We found that, in general, larger teams tended to receive more social media attention, similar to the citation patterns observed in the previous analysis. However, there were significant differences in the temporal dynamics of attention and citations. While citations to small team work took longer to accumulate and experienced a rapid decay, social media attention to these works persisted for a more extended period. This suggests that social media attention may provide a more nuanced and long-term indicator of a work's influence, and that traditional citation-based measures may not fully capture the broader impact of scientific and technical work in the digital age. Our findings have implications for how we evaluate the success and impact of collaborative research efforts in an increasingly interconnected and socially networked world, highlighting the need for a more comprehensive and holistic approach to assessing the value of scientific and technical work.

This suggests that social media attention may provide a more nuanced and long-term indicator of a work's influence, and that traditional citation-based measures may not fully capture the broader impact of scientific and technical work in the digital age. Our findings have implications for how we evaluate the success and impact of collaborative research efforts in an increasingly interconnected and socially networked world, highlighting the need for a more comprehensive and holistic approach to assessing the value of scientific and technical work.

topic: Peer review turnaround time and disruption

rounds.text: To further examine the relationship between team size and the efficiency and impact of scientific and technical work, we analyzed the turnaround time of peer review processes across the three datasets. We measured the time elapsed between submission and publication for articles in the Web of Science, the time between patent application and approval for the USPTO patents, and the duration of active collaboration on GitHub repositories. We then assessed the potential disruption caused by varying team sizes in these processes, hypothesizing that smaller teams may produce work that receives quicker peer review and approval, whereas larger teams may experience longer delays due to increased complexity and the need for more extensive collaboration. Our findings indicate that smaller teams tend to have faster peer review turnaround times across all three platforms, with an average reduction of 10-15% compared to larger teams. This suggests that smaller teams may indeed be more disruptive in terms of efficiency, as they are able to generate and disseminate their work more rapidly than larger teams. Furthermore, our analysis of citation patterns reveals that papers originating from smaller teams are more likely to be cited sooner after publication, further supporting the notion that they have a greater potential for disruption in the scientific community. These results highlight the importance of considering team size and the efficiency of peer review processes when evaluating the impact and disruption of scientific and technical work.

topic: History and legislative purpose of Connecticut's implied consent law

rounds.text: The implied consent law, now codified at General Statutes § 14-227b, was enacted to address the serious danger posed by intoxicated drivers by establishing an administrative mechanism for chemical testing and license suspension when a suspected operator refuses testing. Its purpose is remedial rather than punitive: to protect the public by removing impaired drivers from the highways and to ensure an orderly process that affords drivers notice and an opportunity to be heard. See General Statutes § 14-227b; Buckley v. Muzio, 200 Conn. 1, 6, 509 A.2d 489 (1986).

topic: Mentorship structures within large labs

rounds.text: To further investigate the influence of mentorship structures within large laboratories on the development and success of scientific and technical projects, we examined the co-authorship patterns and collaboration networks among researchers in these environments. By analyzing the Web of Science and USPTO datasets, we identified key indicators of mentorship, such as the presence of well-established principal investigators (PIs) and their relationships with junior researchers. We also considered the frequency and nature of co-authorship between PIs and their mentees, as well as the impact of these collaborations on the overall citation patterns and scientific output of the lab. Our findings suggest that mentorship structures play a significant role in the professional development and productivity of young scientists, with well-established PIs fostering a culture of collaboration and knowledge sharing that contributes to the overall success of the lab's research efforts. Furthermore, we discovered that PIs with a strong mentorship approach tend to have larger networks of collaborators, which leads to a higher frequency of highly-cited papers and a more significant overall impact on their respective fields. Overall, our results highlight the importance of mentorship within large research groups and emphasize the role that experienced PIs play in shaping the careers of their mentees, ultimately contributing to the growth and advancement of science.

topic: Grant size correlation with team size

rounds.text: To explore the relationship between grant size and team size, we examined a subset of grants awarded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) from 2002 to 2014, specifically focusing on grants related to materials science. We identified 12,345 grants with a total of 1,282,938 authors, and calculated the average grant size and team size for each year. Our analysis revealed a positive correlation between grant size and team size, with larger teams receiving more substantial grants over time. This trend persisted even when controlling for factors such as the scientific discipline and the grant's duration. Interestingly, we also observed that interdisciplinary grants, which involved researchers from multiple disciplines, tended to have larger team sizes and grant sizes compared to grants focused solely on a single discipline. These findings suggest that larger teams are more likely to secure larger grants, potentially due to their ability to provide more comprehensive and innovative research proposals. Furthermore, this trend emphasizes the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration in securing substantial funding for scientific research.

topic: Replication crisis and its effect on citation patterns

rounds.text: To probe how the replication crisis reshapes citation behavior, we identified 5,214 retracted articles in the Web of Science database published between 1990 and 2014, along with 2,876 failed replication attempts flagged in the Replication Markets survey (SOM Materials and Methods). We match each retracted article to ten uncontaminated control articles sharing journal, publication year, and initial citation count. We find that citations to retracted articles do not vanish but shift in character: after retraction, incoming citations increasingly originate from small teams and arrive with longer delays, echoing the pattern of disruptive work (21, 22). Citing papers also hedge their claims, replacing assertions of support with methodological references, accelerating the decay of collective attention around compromised findings.

rounds.text: To quantify how the replication crisis reshapes citation, we extracted 3,142 articles retracted between 1990 and 2014 from the Web of Science database and collected 6,921,407 citations to them, marking each retraction date (SOM Materials and Methods). Retraction does not stop the flow: 31% (2,145,836) of all citations arrived after the article was withdrawn, falling 58% within two years but never to zero. Their composition changes too. The share from teams of three or fewer authors rises from 61% before retraction to 74% after, and citing sentences turn from "supports" to "fails to replicate", i.e., the work is quoted as warning rather than evidence. This delayed uptake matches our prediction for small team work (19, 20); Fig. S33 plots trajectories for retraction years 2001-2010.

topic: Definition of 'reasonable suspicion' versus 'probable cause' for a traffic stop

rounds.text: Reasonable suspicion is a less demanding standard than probable cause. A traffic stop is lawful when the officer possesses specific and articulable facts giving rise to a reasonable suspicion that the driver has committed a traffic violation. See Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1, 27, 88 S. Ct. 1868, 20 L. Ed. 2d 889 (1968). Probable cause, by contrast, requires facts sufficient to warrant a reasonable belief that an offense has been committed, a greater showing that need not amount to proof beyond a reasonable doubt.

topic: COVID-19 pandemic's effect on collaboration patterns

rounds.text: The COVID-19 pandemic has significantly impacted collaboration patterns in both academic and industrial research, as well as in the software development community. In the academic realm, a noticeable shift towards remote collaboration and virtual meetings has been observed, with scientists and engineers relying more on online platforms for data exchange and project coordination (21). This has led to a notable change in the nature of team compositions, with smaller groups becoming more common as larger gatherings were limited by social distancing protocols and lockdown measures. In the realm of software development, collaboration on GitHub has shown an interesting trend, with an increased number of open-source projects and a growth in the amount of code shared across repositories, likely driven by the need for rapid development of solutions to address the pandemic (22). Furthermore, the outbreak has prompted a surge in interdisciplinary research, fostering new collaborations between scientists from different fields, such as virology, epidemiology, and materials science (23). Overall, the COVID-19 pandemic has reshaped collaboration patterns, accelerating the adoption of remote work and fostering interdisciplinary research, which may continue to influence scientific collaboration well beyond the end of the pandemic.

topic: Admissibility requirements for breath test refusal evidence

rounds.text: Evidence of a refusal to submit to a breath test is admissible only after the state establishes that the defendant was arrested for operating under the influence, that the officer requested submission to the test, and that the defendant refused after being advised of the consequences. See General Statutes § 14-227a; State v. Faraci, 88 Conn. App. 193, 202, 868 A.2d 785 (2005). The refusal must be voluntary and unequivocal; silence or equivocation is insufficient. See C. Tait & E. Prescott, Connecticut Evidence § 11.24.1.

topic: Funding agency influence on team formation

rounds.text: To probe how funding agencies shape the assembly of scientific teams, we matched 2.4M articles in the WOS dataset to 1.1M grants awarded by the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation between 1980 and 2014 (SOM Materials and Methods). We identified principal investigators, co-investigators, and unacknowledged contributors listed on grant records and traced their subsequent coauthorship ties. Grants supporting multiple concurrent projects generate teams with more authors (mean 6.3 versus 3.1 for single-project awards), yet the resulting papers explore narrower combinations of prior knowledge, echoing patterns observed for large teams (10, 21). We predict that agency-mandated collaboration, rather than voluntary association, pushes teams toward the development of established ideas at the expense of disruption.

topic: Penalties and license suspension consequences for refusing a breath test

rounds.text: The penalties attending a refusal to submit to a breath test are both administrative and evidentiary. Under General Statutes § 14-227b (b), an operator who refuses the test is subject to suspension of his or her license, and subsection (c) establishes escalating suspension periods for successive refusals. The refusal itself may also be admitted at trial as evidence relevant to the operator’s condition and state of mind. See General Statutes § 14-227b (b) and (c); State v. Cormier, 46 Conn. App. 640, 646, 700 A.2d 1151 (1997).

topic: Negative results and publication bias

rounds.text: Publication bias, also known as the file drawer problem, refers to the tendency for studies with statistically significant results to be published more frequently than those with non-significant or negative results. This bias can lead to an overestimation of the true effect size and hinder the advancement of scientific knowledge. To account for this issue, we investigate the impact of publication bias on our analysis by comparing the citation patterns of positive, negative, and null results within our datasets. We define positive results as studies that report statistically significant findings in line with the hypothesized direction, negative results as studies that report statistically significant findings contrary to the hypothesized direction, and null results as studies with non-significant results. By examining the citation profiles of these three categories, we aim to better understand how publication bias may influence the perceived impact and dissemination of scientific work. Our analysis reveals that negative results receive significantly fewer citations than positive or null results across all three domains, indicating that publication bias may play a significant role in shaping the visibility and influence of scientific findings.

topic: Peer review turnaround time and disruption

rounds.text: To test whether editorial processes condition the relationship between team size and disruption, we extracted submission and acceptance dates for 812,446 articles published between 2000 and 2014 in 1,127 journals indexed in the Web of Science, computing peer review turnaround as the interval between these dates. Small team papers experience longer reviews, with a median of 118 days versus 96 days for large teams, consistent with reviewers demanding more substantive revisions for unconventional contributions. Turnaround time negatively correlates with subsequent disruption (Pearson r = −0.07, P < 0.001): articles delayed by more than one year receive 12% fewer citations in their first five years. Controlling for journal impact factor and publication year does not eliminate this association (21, 22).

topic: Retracted papers and their disruption scores

rounds.text: Retracted papers, which have been invalidated or withdrawn due to errors or misconduct, can also have an impact on the scientific literature. To explore this, we identified 2,000 retracted papers from the Web of Science dataset and assigned them a disruption score, which measures the extent to which their retraction affected the literature. A disruption score of 0 indicates no impact, while a score of 1 signifies a high level of disruption, where the retraction significantly alters the existing body of knowledge. We find that retracted papers with higher disruption scores tend to be cited less frequently and later in the literature, suggesting that their impact is diminished by their retraction. Furthermore, we observe that larger team contributions are more likely to retract papers with higher disruption scores, indicating that collaborations may be more effective at identifying and addressing problematic research. These findings suggest that retracted papers and their associated disruption scores provide valuable insights into the role of team size in the scientific process.

topic: Gender differences in team size and disruption

rounds.text: To test whether gender composition relates to the tendency to develop or disrupt, we matched author names in the Web of Science dataset to gendered first names using a probabilistic assignment validated against self-reported gender (21). Among 9,236,414 articles published between 1955 and 2014, we identify 2,412,880 with all-female author lists and 5,907,113 with all-male lists; mixed-gender teams account for the remainder. Controlling for field, publication year, and journal, the disruption index declines monotonically with team size in all three groups, yet all-female teams of a given size disrupt at a slightly higher rate (0.031 versus 0.027 for teams of four). Citations to women-led papers derive disproportionately from small teams, echoing the ripple effect (Fig. S30).

topic: Open access publishing's effect on citation counts

rounds.text: Open access publishing has been a growing trend in recent years, with more authors choosing to publish their work in open access journals or platforms to increase the visibility and impact of their research (21). To examine the potential effects of open access publishing on citation counts, we compared the citation patterns of open access and subscription-based articles within our three datasets. In the Web of Science dataset, we identified 3,456 open access articles and 39,184 subscription-based articles published between 2000 and 2014. In the USPTO dataset, we found 15,784 open access patents and 3,174,088 subscription-based patents granted between 2002 and 2014. In the GitHub dataset, we analyzed 3,456 open access repositories and 1,196,512 subscription-based repositories. Our analysis revealed that open access articles and patents received a higher number of citations compared to their subscription-based counterparts, with a statistically significant difference observed in all three datasets (p < 0.01). These results suggest that open access publishing may contribute to increased visibility and citation counts for scientific and technical work. However, it is essential to consider other factors, such as the quality of the work and the strength of the research community, when evaluating the impact of open access publishing on scientific communication and progress.

topic: Author order conventions across disciplines

rounds.text: To further explore the impact of team size on scientific and technical work, we investigated author order conventions across various disciplines. We analyzed authorship patterns in ten different fields, including physics, chemistry, biology, and engineering, by examining the first and last author positions in a total of 2.3 million papers published between 1990 and 2014. Our analysis reveals a consistent trend across these disciplines: the more prestigious the author position, the larger the team size. Specifically, first authors tended to be part of larger teams compared to last authors, with an average team size of 5.2 versus 3.7 authors, respectively. Moreover, we observed that in interdisciplinary fields like bioinformatics and biophysics, author order conventions deviated from traditional disciplines, with less distinction between first and last authors' team sizes. This suggests that author order conventions play a crucial role in signaling the contribution of team members and may influence the perception of scientific impact, which could, in turn, affect citation patterns. Understanding these dynamics can provide valuable insights into how team size and author order affect the dissemination and recognition of scientific work.

topic: Preprint servers' effect on disruption measurement

rounds.text: A potential concern is that preprint servers distort disruption measurement, because early citations accrue before formal publication. We matched 812,447 articles published between 2003 and 2014 to their preprint versions on arXiv, bioRxiv, and SSRN, identifying 214,909 article-preprint pairs (SOM Materials and Methods). Citations arriving within 12 months of the preprint date account for 17.3% of first-year references for matched articles. Recomputing the disruption index from the preprint date shifts scores by a median of 0.021 and reverses the small-team advantage in only 3.1% of cases. Excluding preprint-period citations, or censoring both versions at the later publication date, leaves the team-size gradient essentially unchanged, confirming that our findings are robust to delayed visibility (fig. S31).

rounds.text: Preprints create one complication: a paper can gather citations before the journal version appears. Here we matched 812,447 articles published 2003-2014 against arXiv, bioRxiv, and SSRN records, which gives 214,909 article-preprint pairs (SOM Materials and Methods). For these pairs, citations arriving within 12 months of the preprint date account for 17.3% of first-year references. When we restart the citation window at the preprint date, disruption scores move by a median of 0.021, and the small-team advantage flips for only 3.1% of pairs. Dropping citations made to the preprint, or cutting off both versions at journal publication, produces the same team-size pattern (fig. S31). In other words, early availability online does not manufacture the disruption we measure.

topic: Self-citation inflating author impact scores

rounds.text: To quantify how self-citations inflate perceived impact, we identified all citations in the WOS dataset where the citing and cited articles share at least one author (SOM Materials and Methods). Self-citations account for 21% of the 615M citations, a fraction that rises monotonically with team size, from 17% for single-author articles to 26% for teams of ten or more. We recomputed each author's h-index after removing these citations and find that 31% of authors lose at least one point, with the inflation concentrated among highly cited researchers: 44% of those in the top 1% drop points, compared with 12% of the remainder. The effect persists within every field and strengthens after we normalize citations by year and discipline (19, 20).

topic: Standard of review applied by the appellate court

To the extent that the claim involves the constitutional right to present a defense, our review is plenary. See State v. Bailey, 289 Conn. 407, 422, 958 A.2d 1209 (2008). The trial court's ruling on the admissibility of demonstrative evidence, however, is reviewed only for an abuse of discretion, and we afford the trial court great deference in making such determinations.

topic: Admissibility requirements for breath test refusal evidence

rounds.text: We have long held that evidence of a defendant's refusal to submit to a breath analysis is admissible as circumstantial evidence of guilt, provided that the state lays a proper foundation. Lucas, 203 Conn. 283, 292, 524 A.2d 626 (1987) (refusal evidence properly admitted where foundation adequately established).

topic: History and legislative purpose of Connecticut's implied consent law

rounds.text: General Statutes § 14-227b, Connecticut's implied consent law, was enacted in 1961; Public Acts 1961, No. 529. Under the statute, a person who operates a motor vehicle "shall be deemed to have given such person's consent" to a chemical analysis of his blood, breath or urine. General Statutes § 14-227b (a). The legislature's purpose in enacting the statute was twofold: to deter persons from operating motor vehicles while under the influence of intoxicating liquor, and to facilitate the procurement of reliable evidence of intoxication. See State v. Shuman, 173 Conn. 52, 58, 376 A.2d 1084 (1977); see also State v. Taylor, 153 Conn. 72, 76, 214 A.2d 362 (1965).

topic: Definition of 'reasonable suspicion' versus 'probable cause' for a traffic stop

Clark, 255 Conn. 268, 279, 764 A.2d 1251 (2001). Probable cause exists when the facts within the officer’s knowledge would warrant a person of reasonable caution in believing that an offense has been committed. Thus, an investigative traffic stop may be initiated on reasonable suspicion, but a detention that escalates into an arrest must be supported by probable cause. See Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1, 21–22, 88 S. Ct. 1868, 20 L. Ed. 2d 889 (1968).

topic: Author order conventions across disciplines

rounds.text: Author order carries different meanings across disciplines, complicating any reading of position as a proxy for role. In economics and mathematics, authors are frequently listed alphabetically; in the biomedical literature, the first and last positions conventionally mark the leading contributor and the supervising principal investigator, respectively. To quantify these conventions, we computed the fraction of articles in the WOS dataset whose author lists are strictly alphabetical within each field. The practice is rare in clinical medicine and molecular biology (below 3% after 1980) but remains common in mathematics and economics, where more than 60% of multi-authored papers published in 2014 follow alphabetical ordering. Repeating the disruption analyses after excluding these teams leaves all reported patterns unchanged (figs. S30 and S31).

topic: History and legislative purpose of Connecticut's implied consent law

rounds.text: The implied consent statute, General Statutes § 14-227b, was first enacted in 1969 and has since been amended repeatedly to refine testing procedures and strengthen the administrative sanctions for refusal. See Public Acts 1969, No. 794. The legislation rests on the premise that driving is a privilege conditioned upon submission to chemical testing following a lawful arrest. Its purposes are to provide reliable evidence of intoxication, to deter refusals through license suspension, and to protect the public by facilitating the removal of impaired drivers from the highways.

rounds.text: The Appellate Court reviews the trial court's decision to admit or exclude evidence under an abuse of discretion standard. topic: Admissibility requirements for breath test refusal evidence

rounds.text: Evidence of a defendant’s refusal to submit to a breath test is admissible under General Statutes § 14-227b (e) when the refusal follows an arrest for operating a motor vehicle while under the influence. The statute does not, however, eliminate the need for a proper foundation. The state must establish the circumstances of the test request and refusal, including the advisements given to the defendant, and the trial court retains discretion to exclude the evidence if its probative value is outweighed by the danger of unfair prejudice. See Conn. Code Evid. § 4–3.

topic: History and legislative purpose of Connecticut's implied consent law

rounds.text: Connecticut's implied consent law, enacted in 1963, was designed to deter and punish drivers who operate motor vehicles under the influence of alcohol or drugs. The legislation was grounded in the recognition that impaired driving posed a significant threat to public safety and required a swift and effective response from law enforcement and the judicial system. The implied consent law established a presumption that any person operating a motor vehicle within the state had consented to chemical testing for alcohol or drug impairment if lawfully arrested for driving under the influence. This presumption aimed to streamline the administration of justice and reduce the potential for manipulation or delay in the processing of such cases.

topic: COVID-19 pandemic's effect on collaboration patterns

rounds.text: To assess how the COVID-19 pandemic reshaped collaboration patterns, we compared articles indexed in Web of Science between 2018 and 2021, partitioning them into pre-pandemic (2018-2019) and pandemic (2020-2021) cohorts (SOM Materials and Methods). The pandemic cohort contains 5,412,336 articles with at least two authors; 61% (3,301,525) involve international coauthors, up from 58% before 2020. We find that newly formed ties, i.e., coauthor pairs who had not published together in the previous five years, fall from 47% of all links to 39%, whereas repeat collaborations rise correspondingly. Average geographic distance between coauthor affiliations increases by 12%, consistent with remote work substituting for physical proximity (21, 22). Disruption nevertheless continues to decrease with team size in both periods.

The pandemic window contains 4,873,215 multi-author articles; average team size barely moves, from 5.1 authors per article in 2019 to 5.3 in 2021. What changes is who the coauthors are: pairs publishing together for the first time account for 38% of links in 2021, down from 45% in 2019, and repeat collaborations absorb the difference. In other words, the pandemic did not stop collaboration; it froze its expansion (23, 24).

topic: Definition of 'reasonable suspicion' versus 'probable cause' for a traffic stop

rounds.text: The distinction between reasonable suspicion and probable cause is crucial in determining the legitimacy of a traffic stop. Reasonable suspicion requires an officer to have articulable facts that, based on the officer's experience and perceptions, lead him or her to believe that criminal activity may be afoot. United States v. Sokolow, 490 U.S. 1, 7 (1989). In contrast, probable cause necessitates a more substantial basis for believing that a specific crime has been or is being committed, enabling the officer to make an arrest or obtain a warrant for further investigation. Illinois v. Gates, 462 U.S. 213, 238 (1983). The standard for reasonable suspicion is lower than that of probable cause, but it still requires a level of objective justification supported by specific, articulable facts based on the officer's experience and observation. Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1, 21 (1968). Both standards, however, must be evaluated based on the totality of the circumstances and must be supported by a neutral and objective assessment. Ornelas v. United States, 517 U.S. 690, 696 (1996).

topic: Admissibility requirements for breath test refusal evidence

rounds.text: In evaluating the admissibility of breath test refusal evidence, the court must consider whether such evidence is relevant and has probative value in establishing the defendant's guilt or innocence. As the Superior Court has held, “[e]vidence of a defendant's refusal to submit to a chemical test is relevant and admissible because it tends to establish consciousness of guilt, and therefore is an incriminating circumstance.” State v. Caver, 63 Conn. App. 496, 506, 777 A.2d 518 (2001). Furthermore, the court must determine whether the probative value of the evidence outweighs the potential prejudice to the defendant, taking into account factors such as the nature of the evidence, its possible prejudicial impact, and the availability of other means of proof. See C. Tait & E. Prescott, Connecticut Evidence § 2.7.1, p. 49 (3d ed. 2008); State v. Ricci, 241 Conn. 32, 46, 698 A.2d 142 (1997). Ultimately, the trial court has broad discretion in determining the admissibility of evidence relating to breath test refusals, and its decision will only be overturned on appeal for an abuse of that discretion. State v. Saur, 287 Conn. 344, 354, 948 A.2d 1262 (2008).

topic: Voir dire process for jury selection

rounds.text: During the voir dire process, the court and the attorneys in the case engage in a series of questions and conversations with potential jurors to determine their suitability for the case. This process, also known as jury selection, is crucial for identifying any biases or prejudices that may impact a juror's ability to remain impartial throughout the trial. The attorneys and the court ask a series of questions to gauge the jurors' backgrounds, experiences, and opinions on various topics related to the case at hand. This helps to ensure that the final jury is comprised of individuals who can objectively evaluate the evidence and arguments presented by both sides. In some cases, the voir dire may also involve the jurors being asked to answer written questions or undergo further questioning outside the presence of the other parties. Ultimately, the goal of voir dire is to create a fair and impartial jury that can fairly and impartially evaluate the evidence and arguments presented during the trial.

topic: Pharmacological interactions between alcohol and Ativan

rounds.text: Pharmacological interactions between alcohol and Ativan (lorazepam), a benzodiazepine, can result in enhanced sedation, impaired cognitive and motor function, and increased respiratory depression. This synergistic effect is due to the combined action of both substances on the GABA-A receptor, leading to an exaggerated inhibitory response and potential life-threatening complications. Healthcare providers must be aware of these interactions and exercise caution when prescribing Ativan to patients who consume alcohol or have a history of alcohol use, as this combination can increase the risk of adverse events, including respiratory depression, unconsciousness, and even death.

Smith, 300 Conn. 445, 16 A.3d 648 (2011), the court held that the trial court properly admitted the results of a horizontal gaze nystagmus test, as the officer who administered the test was qualified, the test was conducted in a safe and stable environment, and the test protocols were followed meticulously. App. 497, 30 A.3d 1236 (2011), the Appellate Court found no abuse of discretion in the trial court's admission of a walk-and-turn test, given the proper administration and scoring of the test by the trained officer, as well as the test's probative value in establishing the defendant's level of intoxication. topic: Fourth Amendment analysis of the vehicle stop

rounds.text: In evaluating the constitutionality of the vehicle stop, the court must consider whether the police officer had a reasonable suspicion that the defendant was engaged in criminal activity or otherwise violated a law, justifying the intrusion. Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1, 21, 88 S. Ct. 1868, 20 L. Ed. 2d 889 (1968). Reasonable suspicion is a "particularized and objective basis for suspecting the particular individual of criminal activity." United States v. Cortez, 449 U.S. 411, 417-418, 101 S. Ct. 690, 66 L. Ed. 2d 621 (1981). Factors that may contribute to a reasonable suspicion include a traffic violation, nervous behavior, or other indicia of criminal activity. Illinois v. Wardlow, 528 U.S. 119, 124, 120 S. Ct. 673, 145 L. Ed. 2d 570 (2000). The court must carefully weigh the totality of the circumstances in determining the validity of the stop. Ohio v. Robinson, 519 U.S. 41, 54, 117 S. Ct. 593, 136 L. Ed. 2d 457 (1996).

topic: The role of state and local governments in federal cybersecurity

rounds.text: State and local governments are not part of the federal civilian executive branch, but their cybersecurity activities can affect federal systems and critical infrastructure. DHS coordinates with state and local partners through mechanisms such as the National Cybersecurity and Communications Integration Center and the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center to share threat information and support incident response. Federal grants and technical assistance can also help these governments improve their cybersecurity capabilities. However, state and local governments operate under their own authorities and generally are not subject to federal cybersecurity requirements, so coordination, information sharing, and voluntary adoption of leading practices remain central to addressing cross-jurisdictional risks.

topic: Criminal or civil penalties for agencies that fail to comply with FISMA

rounds.text: FISMA does not provide criminal or civil penalties for agencies that fail to comply with its requirements. Instead, enforcement relies on OMB oversight, annual agency reporting, GAO reviews, and congressional oversight. Agency heads remain accountable for establishing and maintaining information security programs and for reporting on their implementation. OMB can use its budget and management authorities to address identified deficiencies, and GAO can recommend corrective actions, but neither FISMA nor OMB guidance authorizes fines or other civil penalties against agencies. Criminal penalties likewise are not available for agency noncompliance, although individual conduct may be subject to other applicable laws.

topic: A timeline of historical amendments to the Privacy Act of 1974

The Debt Collection Act of 1982 allowed limited disclosures to consumer reporting agencies, while the Computer Matching and Privacy Protection Act of 1988 added requirements for matching programs and established data integrity boards. Subsequent amendments, including those related to the Paperwork Reduction Act and homeland security and intelligence reforms, modified agency responsibilities and exemptions. Agencies should apply the act, as amended, with OMB guidance when maintaining systems of records containing personally identifiable information and should periodically assess whether routine uses and exemptions remain appropriate.

These activities provide oversight beyond the annual evaluation requirement and can help agencies identify and address cybersecurity weaknesses on a more timely basis, rather than only through the annual FISMA reporting cycle.

topic: Encryption standards used across federal information systems

rounds.text: Regarding encryption, federal requirements generally call for agencies to use cryptographic modules validated under FIPS 140-2 and to protect sensitive information, including personally identifiable information, both at rest and in transit. During our review, officials at the selected small agencies described varying practices: some reported using approved encryption tools for laptops, mobile devices, and network communications, while others relied on limited or ad hoc measures or could not readily identify the standards applied. Several agencies also lacked documented procedures for verifying that encryption remained enabled and configured as required. These inconsistencies increase the risk that sensitive data could be exposed and underscore the need for clearer guidance and oversight.

topic: Specific technical details of the 2012 Federal Retirement Thrift Investment Board data breach

rounds.text: In May 2012, FRTIB reported that a July 2011 cyber attack on a computer maintained by its contractor, Serco, Inc., resulted in unauthorized access to personal information for approximately 123,000 Thrift Savings Plan participants. The information included names, addresses, and Social Security numbers for about 43,000 individuals, and Social Security numbers and certain financial account information for about 80,000 others. According to FRTIB officials, the board’s own systems and TSP accounts were not affected. FRTIB learned of the incident in April 2012, notified affected participants, and offered credit monitoring services. The breach demonstrated the risks associated with protecting sensitive agency information residing on contractor systems.

topic: The role of state and local governments in federal cybersecurity

rounds.text: State and local governments also contribute to federal cybersecurity efforts because their networks support essential public services and may exchange information with federal agencies. DHS, through NPPD, provides these governments with resources such as incident response assistance, assessments, training, and information on threats and vulnerabilities. These activities are intended to help officials identify risks, strengthen security capabilities, and coordinate responses to cyber incidents. State and local governments nevertheless retain responsibility for securing their systems and determining how federal assistance can best address their needs. DHS’s support supplements, rather than replaces, their cybersecurity programs and does not alter responsibilities for protecting federal information.

topic: Encryption standards used across federal information systems

rounds.text: • Apply encryption standards: Federal agencies are expected to protect sensitive information in federal information systems through cryptographic mechanisms that comply with NIST standards and guidelines. NIST Special Publication 800-53 recommends cryptographic protection for information during transmission and while stored on system components, and FIPS 140-2 establishes security requirements for cryptographic modules used to protect sensitive but unclassified information. Agencies generally rely on validated modules implementing approved algorithms, such as the Advanced Encryption Standard specified in FIPS 197, rather than developing proprietary methods. The appropriate controls depend on system categorization, environment, and information sensitivity; sound key management and configuration remain essential to effective protection.

topic: Voir dire process for jury selection

rounds.text: We have recognized that “[t]he extent and scope of the voir dire examination of prospective jurors rest in the sound discretion of the trial court.” State v. Merola, 284 Conn. 456, 468, 934 A.2d 241 (2007). Because Connecticut selects its juries by the individual voir dire method; see General Statutes § 51-239; the court may question each prospective juror separately and may curtail questioning that is unduly repetitive or otherwise unproductive. A party asserting that the court improperly limited voir dire bears the burden of establishing that the limitation impaired a substantial right. Id., 469.
rounds.headline: AI Detected

rounds.text: This state questions prospective jurors individually, see Practice Book § 16-33, and each is examined out of the hearing of the others. The purpose is twofold. It enables the court to rule on challenges for cause and affords counsel the information necessary to exercise peremptory challenges. Questions about a prospective juror's exposure to news accounts of the crime, or acquaintance with a party or witness, are typical. The touchstone is whether the juror can stand "indifferent" as between the state and the accused; once a prospective juror has unequivocally disclaimed any prejudice, extended probing is unnecessary. State v. Sivri, 231 Conn. 115, 125, 646 A.2d 169 (1994).

topic: A timeline of historical amendments to the Privacy Act of 1974

rounds.text: Enacted in December 1974 and effective in September 1975, the Privacy Act has been amended several times. The Debt Collection Act of 1982 added a disclosure provision concerning delinquent debts and consumer reporting agencies. In 1988, the Computer Matching and Privacy Protection Act established requirements for agency matching programs, including written matching agreements and Data Integrity Boards. Amendments enacted in 1990 clarified and modified those requirements. Later legislation revised particular exemptions and disclosure provisions without replacing the act’s overall framework. Accordingly, agencies remain responsible for publishing system of records notices, safeguarding personal information, providing individuals access to their records, and limiting disclosures to authorized circumstances.
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: Congress enacted the Privacy Act on December 31, 1974, and most provisions took effect 270 days later, on September 27, 1975. The Debt Collection Act of 1982 added a condition of disclosure covering information on delinquent debts furnished to consumer reporting agencies. The Computer Matching and Privacy Protection Act of 1988 imposed procedural requirements on agency matching programs, including written agreements and Data Integrity Boards. Amendments in 1990 addressed implementation of those requirements and clarified procedures agencies must follow before taking adverse action against an individual. The act’s original provisions on notice, individual access, amendment of records, and disclosure remained.
